session: How Search works and where's AI?
speaker: Cherry Prommawin, Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: For classic Search, crawling means Googlebot, scheduling and robots.txt, with AI used in parts such as scheduling. Indexing is one big but not limitless index that calculates signals and understands more than words, with AI such as BERT. Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google received close to 200 submissions for the community lightning talks of the Deep Dive, reviewed them over about a month, and gave each selected community speaker seven minutes on stage.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google's hosts said the lightning talks exist because the SEO community holds a lot of knowledge, some of it untapped, and highlighting the people who have it serves the community best.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: A community speaker's approach to AI in agency SEO work is to use it where it meaningfully elevates and enriches existing work rather than replacing it, keeping full strategic oversight and control of the output.
quote: Human judgment and strategy is the default, and AI simply pushes it at scale.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: Asking AI to produce whole SEO deliverables from scratch, such as creating content or auditing a website, is where people get stuck; break a task into its elements and decide where AI can and should play a part, a community speaker advised.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: A community speaker designs AI-assisted deliverables like a flowchart, keeping guardrails in place and keeping the prompts succinct and measured, so the team controls the process end to end.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: In an agency's competitor keyword analysis, a deliverable defined before AI, the team set the strategy buckets and the keyword scoring metrics itself and used AI only to pull in the data, never to make a judgment.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: With AI pulling in the data, a competitor keyword analysis covering 26 competitors and 79 data points per keyword went from three days of work to a few hours, a community speaker reported for his agency.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: For a content audit of a client blog with over 3,000 posts, an agency defined the parameters, scoring and weightings manually and had AI apply them, producing posts grouped by category, possible cannibalisation flags, a priority list and a list of posts to check by hand.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: The key lesson of a community talk on AI automation: AI should not decide what good looks like; people set the rules for what is good and AI applies them.
quote: it didn't decide what good looked like. We did that.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: In a post-migration analysis of over 200,000 lines of search traffic data and more than 45,000 pages, where many URLs had been merged into one, an agency set the rules for what counted as the same page and used AI to match old and new addresses and roll the traffic up per page.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: A community speaker builds SEO recommendations without AI and then uses AI to turn them into mock-ups and visuals, which help win buy-in from clients and internal teams.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: James Powley
label: stage
text: An agency built its own AI visibility tracking tool so it could control the methodology: the team wrote pages of flowchart-style prompts (if this happens, do that) and tested manually, and AI only generated the code.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: A community speaker's example of an LLM error on Search Console data: a chatbot called an average position that went from 8 to 9 an improvement, although position 1 is the top, so the move from 8 to 9 is a decline.

sources.title: What are impressions, position, and clicks?

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: How often an LLM gives a wrong answer about data depends on the model, but how often the mistake is noticed depends on the person using it, a community speaker said.
quote: how often can you notice the mistake? And that depends on you.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: In agency marketing-data pipelines, as in financial forecasting, one misplaced figure travels downstream and compounds into later analysis and decisions, which is why LLM errors on search data must be caught early, a community speaker warned.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: A community speaker reported that a code refactor of his company's AI analysis product left data fetching correct but made the analysis shallow while the answers still read well, with the same model, so polished output is no proof of correct analysis.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: The first rule for using LLMs on search data, according to a community speaker, is never to let the model check its own output.
quote: not let the model grade its own homework

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: A community speaker's first guardrail for LLM answers about data is a receipt: every figure the model gives must be traceable to the data request behind it, so the answer can be verified.
quote: If there is no receipt, there is no reimbursement.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: In a community speaker's verification system, each claim in an LLM's data answer is marked verified, flagged (a hallucination), or skipped or not found.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: Claims that cannot be verified go to a judge, models from other vendors that score them; a failing claim is struck through with the reason shown, and the system annotates and proposes corrections rather than rewriting the answer, a community speaker described.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: Give an LLM your metric definitions as fixed, protected context, for example that position 1 is the top, and leave nothing for the model to guess, a community speaker advised.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: Before using AI-generated numbers, for example in a client meeting, always ask the AI for the receipts and the reason behind every number, because AI hallucinates; LLMs present their reasoning as a forward chain, so the user has to check it backwards, a community speaker said.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community demo showed a script that opens Chrome with a saved session, pastes a URL into Google's Rich Results Test, waits about 15 seconds, then screenshots and saves the result and retries on failure (the demo's recording is largely unintelligible; the tool name is a best reading).

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: In a community demo, a fix loop gave a large LLM (Claude Opus) the current markup, the errors Google's test reported and Google's documentation, had it write new JSON-LD and re-ran the test, with at most three attempts; the demo's page passed on the second.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community demo treated warnings in Google's structured-data test as not critical, in an example result of 22 items with two errors and two warnings.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community demo matched model size to the task: a small, cheap model (Claude Haiku) chose keywords from a page's URL, title, H1, description and schema types, while a large, expensive model (Claude Opus) fixed code and wrote the summary.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: At a community speaker's agency, monthly client reports took each SEO manager one full workday every month, contained technical errors and were not read by anyone, which led the team to automate them.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: To automate SEO reporting with AI-assisted coding, a community speaker advised against aiming for an app or a perfect dashboard: pick one repetitive task, define the smallest useful output, ask the AI what is possible, then build and debug one step at a time.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: A community speaker who is not a developer automated monthly SEO reports with Python in Visual Studio Code, using Claude and ChatGPT as coding partners and Google Cloud for access to the Search Console API.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: An agency's automated monthly SEO report follows four simple steps: the data comes in, a script processes it, AI summarises it and the result goes onto a dashboard.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: Before writing code to pull Search Console data for one property, check which data you actually need, what the API can provide and what the API costs, a community speaker advised.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: Pulling Search Console data through the API required setting up a Google Cloud account to get API access, a community speaker said.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: A community speaker gave the AI a detailed description of the tech stack and requirements and started tiny, with one script, one client and one output, before having the AI write the code.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: When debugging AI-written code with AI, always read the code and understand what went wrong, so you can fix it yourself next time, a community speaker advised.
quote: Don't trust it blindly, and try to understand what is happening in your code

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: A good AI summary in an automated SEO report needs cleaned, good-quality data, a clear definition of what is wanted and a detailed, explicit prompt, a community speaker said.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: The resulting monthly report showed Search Console data on one side and an AI-written summary of what happened that month on the other; an in-house AI specialist built the dashboard from the SEO manager's code.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Kira Breuer
label: stage
text: To start automating SEO work with AI, a community speaker said you need no expertise, only one painful task, a clear outcome and the patience to iterate.
quote: you don't need to be an expert; you just need to try.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Search Console Help defines position as the position of a link on Google, where 1 is the topmost position, and says the Performance report shows the topmost position a property's link occupied, averaged across all queries.

sources.title: What are impressions, position, and clicks?

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Search Console Help separates critical issues, which make a structured-data item invalid and stop it from appearing as a rich result, from non-critical issues, listed under 'Improve item appearance'; the Rich Results Test reports valid items that have warnings.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Google Search Console API documentation
label: docs
text: To use the Search Console API you need a Google Account with Search Console permission on the property, a project in the Google API Console and OAuth2 credentials (all Search Console APIs except the Testing Tools API need OAuth2).

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Google Search Console API documentation
label: docs
text: Google states that all use of the Search Console API is free of charge but subject to usage limits.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Author's view: the Search Console API itself costs nothing, so the cost check advised on stage before automating reports is about the API's usage limits and the paid parts of the pipeline, such as storage and AI model calls.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Author's view: an LLM fix loop that stops when Google's test passes proves only that the JSON-LD is valid, not that its values are true; Google's generative AI content guidance asks for AI-generated structured data to be fact-checked as well as validated.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker framed the web as now visited by both humans and AI agents, so sites have to be prepared for both.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said llms.txt files are not necessary, citing a third-party study from summer 2026 (heard as Ahrefs') that looked at almost 40,000 sites over one month: 97% had no AI agent hits on the file, and those that had any got about two hits a month.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker advised against publishing markdown copies of HTML pages for AI agents: the copy is a duplicate (which the speaker also called a possible source of cloaking, an uncertain word in the recordings), and the models are trained to read HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker pointed out that, according to Google's documentation, user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a page because a user asked for it, generally ignore robots.txt rules.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said AI agents understand a page through a combination of three inputs: a screenshot, the DOM (the HTML plus the changes rendered by JavaScript) and the accessibility tree.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said layout shifts, such as a button or image popping in after the first load, annoy users and may confuse AI agents, and recommended watching Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), the Core Web Vitals metric for visual stability.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said schema markup helps AI agents interpret a page: on a product page, marking up which number is the price saves the agent from guessing.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker advised keeping headings inside the main content in a logical hierarchy (title, section subtitles, subsections) so agents can follow its structure, avoiding several H1 elements and skipped levels such as an H3 followed directly by an H5.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said a block of content without semantic HTML or landmarks is just a div whose purpose an agent cannot tell, and recommended landmark elements (header, nav, main, article for independent sections, footer) plus p and h1-h6 for text.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker described ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) as a set of attributes, not a programming language, that adds accessibility information to HTML: a div used as an 'add to favourites' button can get role=button, an aria-label and aria-pressed set to true or false.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker warned that no ARIA is better than bad ARIA: wrong or confusing ARIA attributes do more harm than leaving them out.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker presented WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) as a way for a site to declare the actions it offers to AI agents, for example booking an appointment in a calendar, so an agent does not have to scrape the interface; the speaker called it faster, easier and cheaper.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said that at the time of the event (30 September 2026) WebMCP was not supported by all browsers but could be enabled for testing through browser flags.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker said WebMCP has two kinds of tools: declarative ones, mostly HTML annotations such as the fields of a contact form, and imperative ones for other actions such as booking, filtering a catalogue, adding products to a cart, getting product specs or reordering.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Carlos Ortega
label: stage
text: A community speaker summed up agent readiness in three layers: a good CLS improves how agents see content, schema, landmarks and ARIA how they understand it, and WebMCP how they interact with it.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker contrasted real audience understanding (reading logs, tracking how the brand is mentioned and perceived, letting customer complaints change pricing pages and products) with keyword-tool research that turns People Also Ask questions into H2s and blog posts.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker said the SEO industry turned everything into a metric because budgets are approved on numbers, not ideas.
quote: an idea doesn't get you budget approval; a number does.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker said not all SEO work was wrong: a site still has to be crawlable and visible before it is even considered, and much of that work is plumbing, not gaming.
quote: There's a lot of plumbing that's not gaming.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker said Google's AMP project, meant to get people building fast websites and addressed directly to engineers and marketers, was smart, but the industry reduced it to a metric and a checklist ('now I have an AMP website').

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker said a third-party study from early 2026 found that websites with JSON-LD were shown much more often, and that the industry reacted by adding schema markup everywhere.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker said a later controlled study, which added schema markup to pages that lacked it and kept everything else unchanged, found only a negative correlation: the markup had been a sign of teams doing everything else right, not a cause.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker said listicles do earn more mentions in AI answers, not because they are trusted more but because LLMs mainly check that the thing being talked about exists, not whether the content is honest.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker suggested that LLMs pick up some of Google's years of work on judging honesty and trust (E-E-A-T) by proxy, because they send many queries (probably fan-out queries) to search engines.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker warned that the SEO industry is overusing listicles for AI visibility the way it once overused links.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker cited a third-party study (heard as Peec AI's) finding that 43% of prompts produced fan-out queries in a language other than the one the user searched in.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker showed a Spanish-language AI prompt about places to eat in Barcelona whose fan-out queries were all in English, so the content used to answer may be written by and for a different audience than the one asking.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Thiago Pojda
label: stage
text: A community speaker argued for adopting the GEO label as the industry's chance to leave behind the bad reputation SEO built, unlike Google's view earlier the same day that the new name is not needed.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker compared traditional search to walking into a store and searching the shelves yourself, and AI search to asking a sales assistant who searches, selects, summarises and presents the answer for you.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker said most AI-visibility tracking copies rank tracking and is worse than it, because it tracks invented prompts with no known search volume.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker proposed measuring AI search as a five-stage funnel (know, association, search, retrieval, selection) to learn whether the AI understands, trusts and finally chooses a brand, measuring the earlier stages rather than only the last.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker said most AI-visibility measurement covers only the selection stage, whether a brand is mentioned or selected, without showing why or why not.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker named two signals that in their view strongly influence whether an AI selects a brand: the bias already in the model's memory before it searches, and the brand's presence in the search results the model is grounded on.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker proposed an 'AI bot allow rate' for the know stage: the share of AI training bots a site allows (three of four is 75%), with 100% as the target.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker advised not blocking AI training bots in most cases, because a model that may not crawl a site finds it harder to represent the brand accurately in its parametric memory.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker described the association stage as whether an AI already connects a brand with the topics that matter to it before running any search, and said problems there are mostly brand problems.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker's 'brand association rate' asks a model, with web browsing switched off so that only its memory answers, to name ten topics it associates with the brand, or the other way round, starting from a topic.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker advised repeating brand-association prompts over time: association in every run is good, in about half the runs shows some association with work to do, and little or none shows a clear gap.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker proposed a 'brand co-occurrence rate' for the search stage: the share of an AI's fan-out queries that contain the brand (one in three is 33%), which also hints at the associations the model already has; problems there are mostly relevance problems.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker said Microsoft is ahead of Google in giving site owners the grounding queries its AI uses.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker described the retrieval stage as whether an AI requests a site's pages when grounding its answer; if it does not, the cause may be a crawling or an indexing issue.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker described the selection stage as whether a brand is chosen in the answer, measured with mentions and similar metrics; failure there is mostly a trust or relevance issue.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Closing the lightning talks on automation and AI, one of the session's Google hosts called AI a tool that can be used well or badly: it can even be used for content generation, which none of the talks featured, and it is fantastic for coding and analysis but less so for other tasks.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: One of the Google hosts of the AI lightning talks advised always checking what AI tools do and focusing on what the business and its users need.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's SEO Starter Guide says headings in semantic order help screen readers but do not matter to Google Search if used out of order, and that there is no ideal number of headings for a page.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: A logical heading hierarchy is not a Google Search requirement, since Google says out-of-order headings do not matter to Search; the case for it is accessibility, where web.dev advises against skipping levels, and agents that read the accessibility tree.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's AI optimisation guide says structured data is not required for generative AI search and needs no special schema.org markup, and on Day 2 Google said raw schema.org is generally not put into model context (D2-C477); use markup for rich-result eligibility and clear data, not as an AI-visibility lever.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Chrome for Developers
label: docs
text: Chrome's WebMCP documentation describes WebMCP as a proposed web standard that site owners can test through an origin trial starting in Chrome 149 or through a Chrome flag for local development.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: Rafael Kovashikawa
label: stage
text: A community speaker applied Pascal's line about makers of false windows built for symmetry, whose rule is to make pleasing figures rather than to speak accurately, to today's LLMs: sometimes they are not trying to produce the most accurate figures or the most accurate interpretations of them.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community demo's script used both input modes of Google's Rich Results Test: the URL mode for public pages, which Google fetches itself, and the code mode, into which the script pasted the page's HTML, for private pages and pages Google cannot fetch (best reading of a largely unintelligible recording; the second kind of page was heard as 'dead', possibly 'dev').

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: In a community demo, the structured-data problems Google's Rich Results Test reported on the test page included an empty name, a breadcrumb problem and a price of zero, with errors shown in pink and warnings in orange (best readings of a largely unintelligible recording; each item is heard in only one of the two recordings).

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: In a community demo, the small model choosing keywords (Claude Haiku) followed fixed rules, no brand terms, no navigation terms and at most two keywords per page; the Spanish example was 'zapatos de mujer' and 'comprar zapatos de mujer' (women's shoes, buy women's shoes).

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The study cited on stage matches Peec AI's analysis (reported in February 2026) of over 10 million ChatGPT prompts and 20 million fan-outs: 43% of the fan-out searches for non-English prompts ran in English, and nearly 78% of non-English prompt runs had at least one English fan-out (from 66% for Spanish to 94% for Turkish), so the 43% is a share of fan-out searches, not of prompts.

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI

label: analysis
text: The llms.txt study cited on stage matches Ahrefs' June 2026 study of 137,210 domains: 28% (about 38,000, the 'almost 40,000' sites heard on stage) published an llms.txt file and 97% of those files received no requests at all in May 2026; the files that were fetched got about 22,000 requests across some 1,100 domains, around 20 each, not the 'two hits a month' heard on stage.

sources.title: We Analyzed 137K Sites: 97% of llms.txt Files Never Get Read

session: Lightning session A: Automation and AI
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's merchant listing documentation lists the product name as a required property and, unlike product snippets, requires a price greater than zero for merchant listing experiences.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: The crawl pipeline runs from a crawl queue to a scheduler to the crawler, which fetches from the internet and passes the fetch reply to indexing.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: The crawler has multiple tasks: fetch from the internet, ensure it doesn't break the internet, and enforce robots.txt policies. Fetched data is sent for indexing.
quote: Ensure we don't break the internet

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: The scheduler is shared infrastructure that decides what to fetch and when and sends URLs to the crawler. Each team decides the scheduling parameters for its own user agents.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google Search, Ads, Shopping and Images all request through one centralised crawling infrastructure, whose primary mandate is to fetch from the internet while strictly preventing the overloading of external servers.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Because every Google product shares the same host capacity, Ads or Shopping fetches that hit a slow server can reduce how much is crawled for Search.

author: Search Central blog (31 March 2026)
label: docs
text: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot currently fetches only the first 2MB of each URL, HTTP headers included (64MB for PDFs); bytes past that cutoff are not fetched, rendered or indexed, and each resource the page loads has its own separate limit.

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

author: Search Central blog (31 March 2026)
label: docs
text: Google's Inside Googlebot post warns that bloated inline base64 images, large blocks of inline CSS or JavaScript, or megabytes of menus can push a page's text or structured data past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff, and advises moving heavy CSS and JavaScript to external files and placing meta tags, the title, the canonical and essential structured data high in the HTML.

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Google's crawling talk opened with how the internet works (TCP/IP, internet service providers, IP addresses, URLs, DNS and HTTP), because crawling can only be understood with that wider scope.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: A URL states how a resource is requested (the protocol, HTTP or HTTPS), where (the host, meaning which computer on the network) and what (the path to the exact page or file).

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: DNS works as the internet's address book: it is consulted for each request and tells the client at which IP address a host name can be reached.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: An HTTP 200 OK status only means that the server believes it managed to do what the client asked for.
quote: just means that the server believes that it managed to accomplish whatever the user was asking for

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes pointed to the Last-Modified and ETag headers as the fields of an HTTP response that matter for caching.

sources.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Googlebot is an ordinary HTTP client with nothing special about it: like a browser, it fetches a URL it was given and returns the fetched bytes to Google's servers.
quote: Googlebot is just a client. It is an HTTP client. There's nothing all that much special about it.

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process
In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: AI agents are, technically, the same thing as crawlers: HTTP clients that accomplish something on behalf of a user or a service.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google runs probably hundreds, if not thousands, of crawlers on its crawler infrastructure; some of them are named and some are not.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Googlebot is the crawler Google uses for web search, including Search's AI features.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google does not let each team build its own crawler: its many crawlers share one crawler infrastructure, because every crawler must accomplish a few specific tasks and obey Google's internal crawling policies.

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google said it does not usually talk publicly about crawl components such as the scheduler and the crawl queue, because the details get confusing and taken out of context.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: During indexing Google extracts the URLs found in fetched content and passes them back to the crawler and the scheduler to be crawled.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Apart from contractual crawlers, all of Google's automated crawlers obey robots.txt, which Google treats as the way site owners opt out of its crawling.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: The only Google-owned crawlers that do not obey robots.txt are contractual crawlers, which crawl a site whose owner has agreed that Google may crawl it however it likes.

sources.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google's crawl scheduler very likely deprioritises a URL when the URL or its site is known to be historically spammy.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: The crawl scheduler logs how often each page changes and crawls frequently changing pages first: a news site's homepage, which changes very often, is prioritised over its terms of service page, which may change once a year.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: The scheduler hands the crawler an ordered list of URLs from the crawl queue, and the crawler works through the list from top to bottom.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Different Google teams prioritise crawling differently: web search cares a lot about the quality of a site and its content, while Ads wants to check every publisher page that wants to appear in Google Ads, so it schedules those URLs as they come in.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Crawling for Gemini may be set to care less about quality and more about the amount of content, because for large language models the number of tokens matters more than quality.
quote: the number of tokens is actually more important

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google finds what to crawl mainly by extracting URLs from previously crawled pages, and additionally from sitemaps.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: An XML sitemap, a format from around 2005, gives Google, other search engines and potentially AI systems a list of the URLs a site wants crawled; Google called it nothing fancy but said it still uses sitemaps.

sources.title: How is a Google Sitemap different from an HTML sitemap?

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google described its crawling as a large-scale distributed swarm of simple HTTP clients, roughly what one would get by deploying many wget or curl libraries on cloud compute instances.
quote: a large-scale distributed swarm of simple HTTP clients

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: To debug crawl issues, Google points site owners to the Crawl Stats report in Search Console, found in the Settings page under Crawl stats.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Search Console's Crawl Stats report shows how much Google crawls from a site, the errors Google received, and the content types fetched by the different crawlers.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes called the Crawl Stats report the most valuable tool for debugging crawl errors, together with server logs, which he called the real thing for those who know how to read them.

author: Search Central blog (31 March 2026)
label: docs
text: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot is today just one user of a centralized crawling platform, and that dozens of other clients, such as Google Shopping and AdSense, send their crawl requests through the same infrastructure under other crawler names, with only the larger ones documented.
quote: Googlebot is just a user of something that resembles a centralized crawling platform

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawler documentation says special-case crawlers serve specific Google products where the crawled site and the product have an agreement about the crawl process, so they may ignore robots.txt rules; AdsBot, for example, ignores the global (*) user agent with the ad publisher's permission.

sources.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: On stage Google spoke of probably hundreds, if not thousands, of crawlers, while its Inside Googlebot post speaks of dozens of other clients; both agree that only the larger crawlers are documented, so a Google user agent missing from the public lists is not proof of a fake request, and reverse DNS or Google's published IP ranges are the test.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: DNS issues and firewalls are blind spots: Google does not know a firewall is blocking it, it only sees that requests fail.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google treats network timeouts, connection resets and DNS errors like 5xx server errors: crawling slows down immediately, and already indexed URLs that stay unreachable are removed from Google's index within days.
quote: Google treats network timeouts, connection reset, and DNS errors similarly to 5xx server errors.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Soft 404s were named as a crawl problem alongside DNS and firewall issues, and described as one of the biggest problems on the internet right now for crawling and showing up in Search.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

author: Google
label: docs
text: 5xx and 429 responses prompt Google's crawlers to slow down temporarily. Already indexed URLs are preserved in the index for a while but eventually dropped.
quote: already indexed URLs are preserved in the index, but eventually dropped

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

author: Google
label: docs
text: 4xx status codes other than 429 have no effect on crawl rate.
quote: The 4xx status codes, except 429, have no effect on crawl rate.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

author: Google, Google Search Central
label: docs
text: A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

author: Google
label: docs
text: If robots.txt returns a 5xx error, Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the cached copy for up to 30 days.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's page on verifying its crawlers says Googlebot and Google's other common crawlers resolve to crawl-*.googlebot.com or geo-crawl-*.geo.googlebot.com host names, special-case crawlers to rate-limited-proxy-*.google.com and user-triggered fetchers to *.gae.googleusercontent.com or google-proxy-*.google.com, and it publishes each group's IP ranges as JSON files such as common-crawlers.json and special-crawlers.json.

sources.title: Verify requests from Google crawlers and fetchers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: HTTP status codes fall into five classes, 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and each class affects crawling differently.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: 1xx informational status codes, which only say that a request was received and more data is coming, have no meaning of their own for crawling.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: When a crawler's request returns 200, the page, file or other resource that comes back is eligible for indexing.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: A 204 No Content response is not eligible for indexing, because the server confirms the request but returns no content to index.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Google follows 3xx redirects, permanent (301, 308) and temporary (302, 307), to the new location, and whether content gets indexed depends on what the redirect target returns.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: A 304 Not Modified response tells Google's crawler that the content has not changed since its last visit.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: 404 Not Found and 410 Gone both tell Google there is nothing at the URL, so the URL is not indexable.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: A 403 response tells Google's crawler it has no permission to see the requested content, so there is nothing for Google to index.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: 429 Too Many Requests is the exception among 4xx codes: instead of meaning there is nothing at the URL, it tells Google's crawler to slow down, and Google slows its crawling.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Google slows crawling when a site returns 5xx errors, because a 5xx usually means the server, and often the whole site, cannot serve requests, and Google does not want to break the site.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: A soft 404 is a 404 in disguise: the page returns 200 but its content says something like 'page not found', information the site should have sent as the HTTP status.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Soft 404 pages are still crawled like normal pages; their bigger consequences are for indexing, and they also affect crawling.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes called DNS and network errors a very common issue on the internet nowadays, and DNS problems very pesky to debug.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: DNS errors get a site removed from Google Search very aggressively, and Search Console alerts site owners to them.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Most network errors happen somewhere between the site's origin server and Google's data centers, where they are invisible to both Google and the site owner; the way TCP networks work leaves no way to see what went wrong there.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: When Search Console reports network errors, the first step Google recommends is to ask the hosting provider, or the CDN, whether they changed anything.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Network timeouts are usually caused close to the site, very often by a firewall, a CDN, the hosting provider or the DNS provider, and Google has no visibility into them.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Network errors and timeouts, like DNS errors, can get a site removed from Google Search and, with it, from every feature that depends on Search.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: For DNS and network errors caused by a firewall or CDN, Google advises checking whether new firewall rules were set recently and otherwise asking in the CDN's forum, as Google itself cannot see or help with these errors.

sources.title: Debug network and DNS errors for Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: A rise in HTTP errors in crawl reports can come from a CDN throttling crawlers by injecting 429 or 503 responses on the network path between Google's crawler and the site.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google treats a 402 Payment Required response as a 404 Not Found, because Googlebot cannot pay for content.
quote: 402 will just mean 404 to us

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Search Console's page indexing report breaks down the reasons why pages do or do not show in Search, and its categories help find patterns in how a site's content is crawled and served to Google's crawlers.

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's status code page says that with a 204 No Content response Google receives no content and cannot process it, and that a 2xx page whose content is empty or an error message shows as a soft 404 in Search Console.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawlers follow up to 10 redirect hops by default (some products' crawlers have other limits); content served by the redirecting URL is ignored and the final target's content is processed instead.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Day 1 said a CDN captcha page served with HTTP 200 becomes a soft 404, while Day 2 (D2-C374, D2-C375) said such challenge pages are hard to recognise as errors and can be clustered as duplicates; Google's CDN post describes both outcomes, and in both the real pages drop out of Search.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google said soft 404s, like some other problem categories, are looked up in Search Console's page indexing report, while other crawl issues are debugged in the Crawl Stats report.

label: slide
text: The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.

author: Google
label: docs
text: Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Google
label: docs
text: When matching rules to a URL, Google uses the most specific rule by path length. If rules conflict, it uses the least restrictive one.
quote: In case of conflicting rules, including those with wildcards, Google uses the least restrictive rule.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Google
label: docs
text: In robots.txt, * matches zero or more of any character and $ marks the end of the URL.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Under the example file, Googlebot may crawl /, /politics/eu-vote and /sports/live/, and is blocked from /?utm_source=x, /index.html, /politics (no trailing slash), /live/ and /sports/live-score. An 'allow: /$' rule does not cover the homepage with tracking parameters.

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours and reads only the first 500 KiB of the file.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
quote: Google-Extended does not impact a site's inclusion in Google Search nor is it used as a ranking signal in Google Search.

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: Googlebot ignores an unknown line, such as a Content-signal line, placed between two user-agent lines and joins both user agents into one group, so the rules that follow apply to both; in the slide's example both are blocked.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: Bing closes the robots.txt group at an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines, so in the slide's example bingbot ends up not blocked while Googlebot is; the slide warned that different crawlers behave differently.
quote: Unpredictability is never a good time.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Content-Signal lines are now common because a large CDN provider adds them to its managed robots.txt files. Never place any non-standard directive between user-agent lines; put it after a group's rules and test the file with each search engine's tools, such as Bing's robots.txt tester and Google's open-source robots.txt parser.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The robots.txt talk pointed to the robots.txt file of thebestfriedchickenever.com to show why comments in robots.txt are useful; the live file is mostly a large ASCII-art drawing written as # comment lines, followed by a single user-agent group (checked 2026-10-04).

author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google's robots.txt talk recalled that robots.txt began in 1994, when bots were crashing servers: Martijn Koster proposed a text file in the root of a site with rules for how automated clients may access it.

sources.title: Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said it already supported robots.txt when it started crawling in 1996 as a Stanford PhD project, and has supported it ever since.

sources.title: Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Robots.txt is now an IETF standard, RFC 9309, supported by basically all major crawlers; Google said it follows it because it is the right thing to do: anyone who wants to opt out of crawling should be able to.

sources.title: Robots Refresher: Future-proof Robots Exclusion Protocol

Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The standard's official name is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP). Google stressed that it was designed in 1994 only to control which automated clients may access what on a site, and has nothing to do with how the content is used.

sources.title: Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Robots.txt is not a security measure: the file sits at a predictable public address, so anyone can read the paths it disallows. Protect a secret folder with authentication, or do not put it on the internet.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The robots.txt file always sits in the root of the host; it cannot be placed anywhere else.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Robots.txt was made extremely simple by design so that anyone could implement and understand it; it was extended as websites grew more complex, but it still has only three rules: user-agent (a named crawler, or * for every crawler), disallow and allow.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification
Robots Refresher: Future-proof Robots Exclusion Protocol

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Everything on a site is implicitly allowed, so an allow rule is only needed to re-open a specific path inside a disallowed one.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Comments in robots.txt start with #, and a line without the # that a parser cannot read is ignored anyway, because the standard requires parsers to skip lines they cannot parse, so it acts like a comment.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In the talk's worked example, disallow /*/live/ blocks /science/live/ and /sports/live/, because * matches any number of characters, and an allow /science/live/ rule re-opens that one path.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: To let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage, use user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$; the $ ends the match, so /$ means only the root path and /cats$ means exactly /cats.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The 'first' needs care: OpenAI documented how to block its GPTBot crawler in robots.txt in August 2023, before Google announced Google-Extended on 28 September 2023. What Google-Extended added was a token that controls AI-training use of pages fetched by Google's existing crawlers, separately from Search; Apple later introduced a similar token, Applebot-Extended.

sources.title: An update on web publisher controls
sources.publisher: The Keyword, Google blog (28 September 2023, Danielle Romain)

sources.title: How to spot OpenAI's crawler bot and stop it slurping sites for training data

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Other companies have similar 'extended' robots.txt tokens; Google named Apple's Applebot-Extended.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google called robots.txt extremely forgiving: a typo in a path only blocks the wrong path, a typo in a rule name such as disallow makes Google ignore that line, and the rest of the file is still used.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The real trouble is an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines: while writing RFC 9309, Google asked people whether the first crawler should then inherit the rules that follow, and opinions split roughly 50-50 (how the talk said the question was settled is unclear in the recording).

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The talk's fix for giving one crawler both an extra rule and the rules of another group: simply add another group for that crawler. Google's spec combines all groups that name the same user agent into one.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said the robots.txt report helps catch CDNs that update a site's robots.txt without the owner's knowledge, and hosts that cloak the robots.txt file, which happens more often than people think.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said the robots.txt report uses the parser Google open-sourced at github.com/google/robotstxt.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.

sources.title: google/robotstxt
sources.publisher: Google (open-source robots.txt parser and matcher library, GitHub)

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Dave Smart
label: stage
text: Dave Smart said robots.txt groups are not additive: if a group matches a crawler's user agent, only that group's rules apply, so a googlebot group that blocks /dogs/ leaves Googlebot free to crawl the /goats/ and /cows/ that the * group blocks.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Dave Smart
label: stage
text: Dave Smart said robots.txt is checked for every URL in a redirect chain and crawling stops at the first blocked one; in his example a site redirected through /cart/ with JavaScript to set the local currency and back, and because /cart/ was disallowed the page was reported as blocked.

speaker: Dave Smart
label: stage
text: Dave Smart said Search Console reports such a block only on the first URL of the chain, which is confusing: the URL shown as blocked by robots.txt is not itself disallowed.

speaker: Dave Smart
label: stage
text: Dave Smart said this applies to all redirects, not only JavaScript ones; his examples: a redirect through an external authorisation service that is blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs over the years with one of them later blocked, and unexpected redirects, such as one served only to Googlebot's user agent.

speaker: Dave Smart
label: stage
text: When Search Console says a URL is blocked by robots.txt but the file does not block it, check whether the URL redirects and test every URL in the chain.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand.
quote: Crawl Budget = Crawl Rate Limit & Crawl Demand

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a host-wide metric shared across all Google crawlers.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others.
quote: high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity available for others

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: If the quality or popularity of a URL is unknown, the aggregate quality or popularity of its parent path is used, then that path's parent, and so on.
quote: If quality or popularity is unknown, use parent root's aggregate quality or popularity is used, then, that path's parent's, and so on.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: New content inherits its starting crawl demand from the folder it sits in. Put new high-value content under sections Google already rates well, not under weak ones.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Crawl budget was described as the attention span Google gives a website, and better performance increases it.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawl budget guide is written for sites with over 1 million unique pages that change weekly, over 10,000 pages that change daily, or many URLs reported as 'Discovered – currently not indexed'.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: On smaller sites, slow indexing is almost always a demand problem, meaning quality, not a capacity problem.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Three things burn crawl budget: server errors unrelated to server load, useless pages and resources, and infinite URL spaces.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.

sources.title: Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Google
label: docs

sources.title: Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Four ways to manage crawl budget: use HTTP cache control, have good site navigation, restrict crawlers' access to faceted navigation and action URLs, and improve or remove useless content.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Google, Search Central blog (9 December 2024)
label: docs
text: HTTP caching for crawlers means supporting conditional requests (ETag with If-None-Match, or Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since) and answering 304 Not Modified when nothing changed. Google's crawling team has said it prefers ETag.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget

label: slide

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Ibrahim Anjro

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
author: Google Search Central

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Crawl budget is the finite amount of resources Google allocates to crawling a specific website, and it determines how many of the site's pages are discovered and how often they are revisited.

sources.title: What Crawl Budget Means for Googlebot

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a proxy for how many requests per second the connection to a site can handle before Google hits the limit.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Googlebot as a single standalone crawler is a historical idea: Google crawls through a centralised crawling infrastructure, so a request from a Google user agent in server logs is a request routed through that shared platform.

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Hostload applies per host, not necessarily per site: depending on how a site is configured, its CDN, its app, its subdomains and its main www host may be different hosts.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget
speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: The quality that drives crawl demand is the quality of the site as a whole, not the quality of an individual page.

session: How Google thinks about crawl budget

speaker: Tobias Schwarz

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The crawler best practices mentioned on stage match the public IETF Internet-Draft 'Crawler best practices' (draft-illyes-aipref-cbcp-00, July 2025), which says self-declared research crawlers, including privacy and malware discovery crawlers, may exempt themselves from any of its practices with a rationale; it is a draft, not Google documentation.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: User-initiated fetchers, such as a translation service fetching a page a user asked to translate, are a different category from crawlers and generally do not check robots.txt, because a user asked for the fetch.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: AI agents acting on a user's request fall into the same category as user-initiated fetchers: an agent told to look at a site reads the page without checking robots.txt.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist argued that it makes business sense for agents not to follow robots.txt: an agent sent to buy something that obeyed a robots.txt block could not complete the purchase, a bad experience for the user and lost revenue for the shop.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said much of robots.txt is written with search engines in mind: a search engine should never add items to a cart or check out, but an agent acting for a user probably should be able to.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked how Google prioritises crawling and indexing for very large real-time sites, such as sports sites, whose content changes constantly and is largely near-duplicate across seasons.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: If a site's server cannot cope with the extra crawling that higher crawl demand brings, Google reduces its crawling of that site again.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked how to tell, from log files or by other methods, whether Google is spending crawl budget inefficiently on a site.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Log files alone cannot show crawl inefficiency because they do not reveal where Google's crawl limit for the site lies; many similar URLs being crawled may not matter if the site is nowhere near that limit.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: To judge crawl efficiency, check Search Console's Crawl Stats report: whether total crawling has plateaued over time, and whether the average response time shows the server is fast enough or is limiting Googlebot.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Log files are worth checking on sites with filter parameters or complicated URLs, because crawlers can easily wander off into URLs that make no sense for the site.

sources.title: Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: One fix for parameter variants of a URL is to work out the normalised URL and redirect the variants to it: the redirects cost crawl budget at first, but leave the site with a clean slate.

sources.title: How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Many crawling complaints that reach Google's crawling team turn out to be caused by a plugin, for example a WordPress calendar plugin that adds calendar parameters to the URLs of every post, page, category and tag page.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google crawls new URLs, such as plugin-generated calendar pages, because it wants to see what they are; its automated systems learn that such URLs are useless only from large samples, which takes time.

sources.title: Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked what changes to expect in Search Console's reporting on Google's AI features.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said he expected more AI reporting to launch in Search Console, without a timeline or a promise, because many people at Google care about giving site owners the information to understand and adapt to what happens in Search.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google said reporting on AI features should not simply mirror classic search results, because users get more information before they click and interact with pages differently, so it first has to work out which data would be useful and actionable.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked for data on AI features as a feedback channel for improving content, as an alternative to prompt-tracking tools.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Query data for AI features is hard to provide because people ask AI very different kinds of questions that do not map back to keywords as in classic search, and the data would have to be grouped to protect privacy while staying useful.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said llms.txt does not matter for Google Search right now and that he does not expect it to, while adding that he had been wrong before.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said llms.txt matters to some people, which is why tools such as Lighthouse add checks for it, so both sides of the debate are right in their own context.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said he knew of no plan for Google to use llms.txt, though it could happen, and that a possible future change is no reason to implement it now.
quote: Just because maybe something will change in the future doesn't mean you should take action now.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said most llms.txt files he had seen are generated automatically by a setting in SEO plugins, so if Google Search ever made llms.txt matter, a site could add one by ticking a checkbox.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist objected that llms.txt is designed for supposedly intelligent systems that should be able to parse a website.
quote: it's designed for allegedly intelligent systems

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist compared llms.txt to the old meta keywords debate: an AI agent should not blindly trust what a site says about its own authority, just as a site calling itself the best car insurance site is no reason to stop looking at others.

author: Chrome for Developers
label: docs
text: Chrome's Lighthouse documentation lists an llms.txt audit among its agentic browsing audits: it flags a server error when llms.txt is fetched and marks the audit not applicable when the file is missing, because providing the file is optional for now.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked whether and when crawl stats will be added to the Search Console API.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google said it knew of no plans to add crawl stats to the Search Console API, because that would be a completely new part of the API.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said adding a report that is a variation of the Performance report to the Search Console API would be easier than adding crawl stats, because the Performance report is already in the API.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google's Search Relations team talks with the Search Console team about the API more than before, partly because with so many vibe-coded systems around it is very easy to just say 'use the Search Console API to do something', and it is annoying when Search Console has no API for that.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said news sites rarely need to worry about crawl budget, because Google crawls them aggressively given their constant flow of new content and new URLs.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: To check that new content is crawled fast enough, Gary Illyes advised measuring the time between publishing a URL and Googlebot's first crawl of it: ideally it stays flat or falls, and only a rising trend calls for investigation.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: When new URLs are picked up more slowly, Gary Illyes advised checking the log files for URLs that Google crawls and recrawls a lot and judging whether they are useful.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience question noted that a cats.txt file received more crawler requests than llms.txt in the server logs and asked how important that is.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: cats.txt was created by an SEO as a satirical take on llms.txt, to show that crawlers fetch whatever files they are given, so requests for llms.txt in server logs do not mean the file is important.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Files such as cats.txt have no importance for Google Search: if a site links to one, Googlebot will find and crawl it, but it has no other effect.
