sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked where the sweet spot is for a sitemap that misses nothing but does not overflow Search Console.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: There is no sweet spot to find for a sitemap: technically it should list every URL you want indexed, so that Google can find each of them.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked how to plan a site migration so that it does not leave large numbers of URLs not indexed.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: In a migration about four or five years before the event, Google consolidated 12 or 14 of its blogs in different languages, a Help Center and its old developers site into one site.

sources.title: Goodbye Google Webmasters, hello Google Search Central

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: The first priority in Google's own site consolidation was to identify the popular URLs people care about and make sure the migration did not damage them.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Where content was duplicated across languages, Google's own site consolidation redirected two language versions into one, giving both old URLs one target path to redirect to.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The consolidation described on stage matches Google's November 2020 move from Google Webmasters to Google Search Central, which moved its main blog, 13 localized blogs and the Search help content of the Search Console Help Center to its developer site: about six years before the event, not the four or five said on stage.

sources.title: Goodbye Google Webmasters, hello Google Search Central

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Nearly all mainstream AI crawlers and AI systems use their own user agents, so robots.txt can set a separate policy for each; at the event OpenAI was said to have three or four, Anthropic a few and Microsoft some.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist doubted that setting different robots.txt policies per AI crawler makes practical sense yet, because nobody knows how these systems will develop.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist called blocking all AI crawlers while allowing search crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot a personal, philosophical decision that every site owner can make.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: To opt out of Google's AI training, a site can use the Google-Extended token in robots.txt.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The panel spoke of blocking Google's 'AI crawling or training' with Google-Extended, but Google documents Google-Extended as a usage token, not a crawler: disallowing it does not stop Googlebot fetching pages and only controls use for Gemini training and grounding.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said Apple offers a robots.txt control for Applebot similar to Google-Extended, so a site can allow Applebot for search while opting out of Apple's AI use.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: When logs show an unknown crawler fetching a lot, search for its user agent online to find the robots.txt token that controls it; the mainstream crawlers that send the most traffic can all be controlled this way.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist called a default-deny robots.txt, which blocks every crawler and allows only chosen ones, a bad pattern because the site owner does not know what is being blocked.
quote: Personally, I think that's a bad pattern, because you don't know what you're blocking.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked what happens to thousands of crawled and indexed paginated category and tag pages if they are replaced by a single page with a JavaScript load-more button, and whether the old pages should then redirect to the canonical first page.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: If paginated pages are replaced by a load-more button or infinite scroll without crawlable links to them, Google will not see the further pages at all.
quote: Googlebot is not running around clicking on buttons

sources.title: Pagination, incremental page loading, and their impact on Google Search

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said the Crawl Stats report's split of crawling by purpose, discovery versus refresh, gives a rough view of whether discovery crawling is in a reasonable range, though measuring publish-to-first-crawl time is more accurate.

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: To check whether Google lowered a site's crawl capacity limit, look at the number of connections Googlebot opens to the site: if it has dropped, the capacity limit changed.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist called pagination one of the trickiest things in web development and said switching to infinite scroll or a load-more button is risky, depending on what you want to achieve, because Googlebot does not click buttons.
quote: the infinite scrolling or load more thing is kind of dangerous, depending on what you want to achieve

sources.title: Pagination, incremental page loading, and their impact on Google Search

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said useless plugin-generated parameter URLs can be handled at the web server, for example with a rule or a custom module in Apache, which saves crawl budget so that Google may pick up the URLs that matter instead (the exact mechanism is not clear in the recording).

sources.title: Managing crawling of faceted navigation URLs

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Asked how to plan a migration that does not leave many URLs unindexed, a Google panelist said the answer is probably not sitemaps: decide what matters from the business's perspective (for example whether to consolidate languages); listing the new URLs in a sitemap is probably a good idea and cannot hurt, but it is not the main tool.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist said, as a fun fact, that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in Google's own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it (the recording does not make fully clear whether the JavaScript performed the redirects or built the mapping).

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said that if the time from publishing to Googlebot's first crawl starts rising, how much it rises matters: for the crawling of fresh stories, something like two hours is probably not great (a smaller example figure is unclear in the recording).

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said that if the Crawl Stats report shows about half of a site's crawling going to discovering new pages, that is a lot of discovery crawling, which suggests that crawling of new pages is not the problem.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear).

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit.

speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said there is no such thing as a duplicate content penalty.

author: Search Engine Journal (8 April 2026)
label: press
text: As reported by Search Engine Journal, John Mueller said in April 2026 that there is no penalty or ranking demotion for having multiple URLs with the same content; Google picks one to keep.
quote: There's no penalty or ranking demotion if you have multiple URLs going to the same content.

sources.title: Google Says It Can Handle Multiple URLs To The Same Content

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.
quote: Some duplicate content on a site is normal and it's not a violation of Google's spam policies.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The real cost of duplicates is control and crawling: Google may choose a canonical you did not want, and every copy is still crawled. Copied or scraped content is a separate spam-policy issue.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's crawlers do not click buttons. Each page in a series needs its own URL and an <a href> link to the next page, should not use page 1 as its canonical, and rel=next and rel=prev are no longer used.

sources.title: Pagination, incremental page loading, and their impact on Google Search

label: stage
text: Images were stressed as important.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: With one in six AI Mode searches being multimodal, original images with descriptive file names, alt text and captions feed AI answers as well as image search.

label: stage
text: Attendees were told to check ARIA and accessibility.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's guide for generative AI features says browser agents may read a site through screenshots, the DOM structure and the accessibility tree, and recommends semantic HTML because it helps users such as screen reader users navigate a page.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google has not called ARIA a ranking signal. The case for it is that AI agents and assistive tools read pages through the same structure: real buttons, labelled forms and semantic headings.

label: stage
text: SEO is not only content; it has many parts.

label: stage
text: Check and focus on rich results for Google.

label: stage
text: Speakers at the event were openly dismissive of llms.txt.

label: stage
text: Googlebot does not support HTTP/3 today.

sources.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawlers support HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, use whichever gives the best crawling performance, and may switch between sessions. HTTP/2 can save server resources but gives no ranking benefit.

sources.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: This does not mean avoiding HTTP/3, which benefits browsers. The rule is never to run a host that only answers over HTTP/3, and to check that CDN or firewall rules written for HTTP/3 traffic do not break HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawler overview says HTTP/1.1 is the default protocol of Google's crawlers and that a site can opt out of crawling over HTTP/2 by answering Google's HTTP/2 requests with a 421 status code.

sources.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)

speaker: audience
label: slide
text: An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google answered on a Q&A slide that good HTML sitemaps are hard to make for large sites.
quote: It's hard to make good HTML sitemaps for large sites.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google's Q&A slide advised large sites to rely on hub pages, such as category pages, that link out to their important pages, instead of on HTML sitemaps.
quote: Better rely on hubs like category pages that link out to your important pages.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
Help Google understand your ecommerce website structure

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google's Q&A slide on HTML sitemaps added that category hub pages linking to a site's important pages have the extra benefit that they may also be useful to users.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's answer did not say whether HTML sitemaps pass link equity. On a large site, check that every important page is linked from a category or hub page in the normal navigation instead of relying on an HTML sitemap page to reach it.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's ecommerce documentation recommends linking from menus to category pages, from category pages to sub-category pages and from sub-category pages to all product pages; where not every product can be linked, it recommends a sitemap or a Merchant Center feed.

sources.title: Help Google understand your ecommerce website structure

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's ecommerce documentation says Google can infer a page's relative importance within a site from its internal links, such as how many links point to the page and how many links Google must follow to reach it.

sources.title: Help Google understand your ecommerce website structure

author: Search Central blog (26 September 2005)
label: docs
text: A 2005 Search Central blog post, now marked as possibly outdated, said Google encouraged HTML sitemaps because they help users navigate a site and a clear hierarchy of text links helps Google index it.

sources.title: How is a Google Sitemap different from an HTML sitemap?

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's view of HTML sitemaps has moved: a 2005 blog post encouraged them, the current sitemap and ecommerce documentation does not mention them, and the 2026 Q&A slide pointed large sites to category hub pages instead.

speaker: audience
label: slide
text: An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google answered on a Q&A slide that whether to keep a temporarily out-of-stock product page or redirect it depends on how important that product page is to users.
quote: It depends on the importance of the PDPs to the users.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google's Q&A slide on out-of-stock product pages said users might wait months for some products, or even pre-order them if the site offers pre-ordering.

sources.title: Temporarily pause or disable a website

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's guide to temporarily pausing an online business recommends that a shop expecting to sell again within weeks or months stays online with limited functionality, such as a disabled cart, and updates its Product structured data to show current availability.

sources.title: Temporarily pause or disable a website

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's redirect documentation says that with a temporary redirect, such as a 302, Google Search shows the source page in search results and does not use the redirect as a signal that the target should be canonical.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Keep a product page that is out of stock for a few months live with a 200 status, show its availability on the page and in Product structured data, and offer pre-ordering where possible when users would wait for the product. Redirect it only when users would rather switch to a similar product than wait.

speaker: audience
label: slide
text: An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
quote: If it's included in the robots.txt file, any crawler can pick your sitemaps up

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google's Q&A slide said that a sitemap not listed in robots.txt has to be submitted instead, for example in Search Console.

speaker: audience
label: slide
text: An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
quote: Simply put, it's because of sites that are extremely important and like to disallow their most important pages, either accidentally or out of ignorance.

speaker: Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.

sources.title: No page information in search results

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's noindex documentation says the noindex rule works only if the page is not blocked by robots.txt: a crawler that cannot fetch the page never sees the rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Explain robots.txt and noindex to developers as two separate controls: robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing. To keep a page out of Search, let Google crawl it and serve noindex; a robots.txt disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's sitemap guide says Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently and verifiably accurate, and counts a change to the main content, the structured data or the links of a page as significant, but not a changed copyright date.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Answering whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, Google said a site that wants one can make one, but that the effort is better spent on hub pages such as category pages.
quote: if you want to make one, knock yourself out, but I will focus on some better things like hub pages, category pages

sources.title: Help Google understand your ecommerce website structure

speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member asked how several sloppy migrations on the same domain can affect Googlebot's crawling.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google answered that several sloppy migrations on one domain can cause many effects in the short term, and noted that migrations concern indexing as well as crawling, a subject a later Day 2 talk would cover.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google contrasted out-of-stock products a buyer will wait for, such as a rare watch battery that matters to them, with easily replaced products, such as a particular cheese, for which the buyer simply picks a similar product instead of waiting.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google said listing the sitemap in robots.txt is fine, as many websites do.
quote: you can include it in robots.txt. No problem whatsoever.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google pointed out the trade-off of listing a sitemap in robots.txt: anyone can then see the sitemap, which a site may not want.

sources.title: How to write and submit a robots.txt file
How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google said very few URLs disallowed by robots.txt are in its index, compared with the index as a whole (no figure given).

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
quote: if a URL is important, then it might get indexed even if it's disallowed by robots.txt. So the URL gets indexed, not the content.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Opening Day 2, Google recapped that Day 1 began with how Search works and then covered crawling, including basics of how the internet works such as TCP/IP, so that attendees could understand how crawlers work.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Google said it strongly believes site owners should be able to opt out of crawling and control how their site is crawled, which can matter for legal reasons or for crawl budget.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's robots.txt introduction names links from elsewhere on the web as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, while on stage Google spoke of the URL's importance; either way, well-linked important URLs are the disallowed ones most likely to appear in results, so keep such pages crawlable with noindex if they must stay out of Search.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: A Google slide titled Data from Crawling showed an example of what the crawler passes on for processing: the fetch result, the connect time and the time to first byte in milliseconds, the robots policies that apply to the fetch, and the raw HTTP response with the page's HTML.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: In Google's example fetch record, the robots policies that apply to a fetch, shown as the value opt-out-google-extended, travel with the fetched page into processing.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: The HTML parsing step turns a fetched page's HTML into a Document Object Model (DOM) tree of elements, attributes and text nodes.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google extracts every element of a page so that it can tell the header, the navigation and the main content apart, and a slide labelled the main content as very important.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Make the main content of every template easy to separate from the header, navigation and footer, for example as one clearly delimited main area, because Google identifies the main content and treats it as the most important part of the page.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Besides the visible content, Google extracts elements that site owners add to the HTML, because they are useful for indexing and, for some of them, for ranking.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
meta tags and attributes that Google supports

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google extracts the rel=canonical link, through which site owners state their preferred canonical URL, and uses it in deduplication and in canonical selection.

sources.title: How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: The rel=canonical link element is placed in the head section of the HTML and tells Google that one page is the representative of another.

sources.title: How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google extracts hreflang annotations, through which site owners specify the language variants of their content, to know whether a page has an equivalent with similar content in another language.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: The speaker said that knowing a page's other-language versions from hreflang is useful in ranking.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Put rel=canonical and hreflang link elements in the head of the HTML the server sends, not only in JavaScript-rendered HTML, so Google can read them during HTML parsing without depending on rendering.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Links and anchors are among the things Google extracts from a page's HTML, and the slide card for them simply read 'We like links.'
quote: We like links.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
meta tags and attributes that Google supports

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: The speaker said links are still an extremely important part of the internet and of most major search and AI systems.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: Google uses the links it extracts for three purposes: discovering new pages, determining a site's structure, and ranking.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google can extract links written as an a element with an href attribute that holds an absolute or a relative URL, which the speaker called the good old normal way.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google cannot extract a link from an a element that only has an onclick handler, because Googlebot does not click, so the JavaScript is never triggered.

sources.title: Pagination, incremental page loading, and their impact on Google Search

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Google cannot extract a link from an href attribute placed on an element other than a, such as a span, because that is not a standard way to make a link.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: A Google slide also listed as not extractable an a element with a routerLink attribute instead of an href, and javascript: URLs such as javascript:goTo('products') or javascript:window.location.href='/products'.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's link best practices say Google can generally crawl a link only if it is an a element with an href attribute, and list routerLink without href, href on a span, onclick-only a elements and javascript: URLs as not recommended, while noting that Google may still attempt to parse them.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's link-extraction slide put routerLink, href on a span, onclick-only links and javascript: URLs under 'can not extract', which is stricter than Google's link documentation saying Google may still try to parse them; either way they are not dependable links for discovery.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Audit every template and JavaScript component that outputs links, such as navigation, pagination, filters and product tiles: each needs a real a element with an href, because onclick handlers, routerLink without href, href on a span and javascript: URLs leave the target pages without a link Google can reliably extract.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: The speaker said Google sometimes also extracts URLs that are typed out as plain text on a page without being hyperlinked; the remarks around this point were unclear in the recording.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Do not rely on plain-text URLs for discovery: even if Google sometimes picks them up, a proper a href link is what was described as feeding discovery, site structure and ranking.

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: slide
text: Links extracted during processing are sent back to the crawl queue, where scheduling starts again for the newly found URLs.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Cherry Prommawin
label: stage
text: The robots meta element is also extracted when Google processes a page's HTML, and the speaker called it probably one of the most important extracted elements, or one the audience is probably interested in.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's page on valid page metadata says that once Google detects an invalid element in the head, it assumes the head has ended and stops reading further elements there; only title, meta, link, script, style, base, noscript and template elements belong in the head.

sources.title: Use valid HTML to specify page metadata

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller noted that robots.txt is defined by an internet standard, RFC 9309, which Google's Gary Illyes co-authored.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification
Robots Refresher: Future-proof Robots Exclusion Protocol
Formalizing the Robots Exclusion Protocol Specification

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said there is currently no RFC that standardises robots meta tags, unlike robots.txt.

sources.title: Robots Refresher: Future-proof Robots Exclusion Protocol

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller encouraged attendees to help write a specification for robots meta tags, saying internet standards groups are made up of ordinary people and need only passion and a willingness to join the discussions.

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: John Mueller opened with a true-or-false quiz slide asking whether robots meta tags can make a page more visible in Search results than having none, and later answered that the statement is true.
quote: You can use robots meta tags to be more visible in Search results than without robots meta tags.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The robots meta tag is a piece of HTML code in the head section of a page that gives search engine crawlers page-specific instructions.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification tells site owners to place the tag in the head section but notes that Google Search does not enforce that placement and also respects robots meta tags in the body of an HTML document.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The primary function of the robots meta tag is to control how a page is indexed and shown in search results.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The robots meta tag is written as <meta name="robots" content="rule1,rule2">, or with the name googlebot instead of robots, with several rules separated by commas.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
meta tags and attributes that Google supports

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said robots.txt does not control indexing, so robots meta tags are what site owners have to use to control it.

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The robots meta rule all is the default value and does nothing: it places no restrictions on indexing the page or following its links, the same as having no robots meta tag, and it is not an instruction that search engines must index the page.
quote: This is the default value - it does nothing

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
meta tags and attributes that Google supports

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The noindex robots rule tells Google not to show the page in search results.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: A slide named internal admin pages, temporary landing pages and thin content as typical use cases for the noindex rule.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: The page-level nofollow robots rule tells search engines not to pass signals to any of the links on the page, which John Mueller called a weird and very broad rule that makes the page stand on its own.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
Evolving "nofollow" – new ways to identify the nature of links

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller recommends rel=nofollow on individual links instead of the page-level nofollow robots rule, so a site can choose which links are useful and which are not.

sources.title: Qualify your outbound links to Google
Evolving "nofollow" – new ways to identify the nature of links

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller suspected that if robots meta tags were reinvented today, the page-level nofollow rule would probably not be part of them.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Audit robots meta tags set by templates and plug-ins: an explicit all rule does nothing and can go, while a page-level nofollow strips link signals from every link on the page and is better replaced by qualifying only the specific links that need it.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said AI crawlers do not really know what to do with nofollow links, because they look at the content rather than building a link graph; he did not say whether he meant Google's AI systems, other AI crawlers or both.
quote: AI crawlers don't really know what to do with a nofollow link, because they're looking at the content

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: The robots rule none is equivalent to noindex plus nofollow, so a page that carries it will not show up in Search, provided Google can see the tag.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification says robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers are found only when a URL is crawled, so the rules on a URL disallowed in robots.txt are never seen and are ignored.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The nosnippet rule stops Google from showing a text snippet or video preview for a page in search results, while the page's title is still shown.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
Control your snippets in search results

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification says that with nosnippet a static image thumbnail, if available, may still be shown when that results in a better user experience.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search.
quote: Also prevents the content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search results.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said Google uses the snippet as a way of building AI Overviews and AI Mode answers, so if a page forbids a snippet, Google cannot use that snippet for them.
quote: we use the snippet as a way of building out the AI Overviews and the AI Mode answers

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's AI features guide says a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, with no additional technical requirements.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Before adding nosnippet or a low max-snippet value, weigh the cost in AI features: both limit how much of the page AI Overviews and AI Mode can use, and John Mueller described those answers as built from snippets.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said data-nosnippet is rarely needed but lets a site keep a specific piece of text, such as a business phone number, out of the snippet, so the page can still be found for it while searchers have to visit the page to see it.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
Control your snippets in search results

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: The data-nosnippet attribute can be used on only a handful of HTML elements.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
meta tags and attributes that Google supports

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: Broken HTML can widen data-nosnippet: if a div marked data-nosnippet is not closed properly, the rest of the page can be blocked from the snippet as well.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification says data-nosnippet may be extracted both before and after rendering, so the attribute should not be added to or removed from existing elements with JavaScript.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said valid HTML is technically not a ranking factor but does matter for controls such as data-nosnippet.
quote: valid HTML is technically not an SEO ranking factor, but it does play a role

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: To hide one detail, such as a phone number, a price or a direct answer, instead of the whole snippet, wrap it in data-nosnippet on a span, div or section in the server HTML and validate the HTML so that an unclosed element cannot hide the rest of the page from snippets.

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The max-snippet:[number] rule limits a page's search result snippet to that number of characters (100 characters, for example), and max-snippet:0 shows no snippet, the same as nosnippet.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said, hedging with 'I think', that the max-snippet limit also applies to AI Overviews and AI Mode.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: A max-snippet value too short for a useful snippet may lead Google to show no snippet at all, John Mueller said.

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: max-snippet:-1 removes the length limit and can produce a longer snippet than having no rule, because by default Google keeps snippets to a length it considers reasonable instead of quoting a page at length.
quote: max-snippet:-1 = No limit. (can be more than without)

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification says Google chooses the snippet length when no max-snippet rule is set, and with max-snippet:-1 chooses the length it believes most effective; it does not say that -1 produces longer snippets.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The max-image-preview rule sets the maximum size of a page's image previews: none shows no preview, standard a default-sized one and large the largest possible, for example in Discover.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said Google Search does not always show an image thumbnail for a result, and when it does, the thumbnail is usually limited to the size of the result entry.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: max-image-preview:large matters mainly in Discover, where it allows a large image that draws people's attention, so the rule can make a page more visible than leaving it out, John Mueller said.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: The max-video-preview rule sets the maximum number of seconds of a video preview in Search; 0 allows only a static image and -1 means no time limit.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said he thinks setting max-video-preview to -1 will not make Google show an hour-long video preview in search results.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller speculated that the use of max-video-preview may change in future, for example in Discover, where letting people view a full video could make sense.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: The notranslate robots rule tells Google not to offer a translation of the page in search results.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said notranslate can also be set in a meta tag named google, and that in that form it also turns off Chrome's automatic translation of the page.

sources.title: Helping you break the language barrier

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's Search documentation gives notranslate as a rule for a robots or googlebot meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header, and says the rule opts a page out of all translation features in Google Search.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Search Central blog (14 October 2008)
label: docs
text: A 2008 Search Central blog post says a meta tag named google with the value notranslate stops Google Translate from translating any of a page's content.

sources.title: Helping you break the language barrier

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said he dislikes notranslate because automatic translation is a form of accessibility for visitors who cannot read the page's language.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: International sites should remove notranslate from their templates unless translation must be prevented: the robots or googlebot form switches off Google Search's translation features, and John Mueller said the form named google also blocks Chrome's translation for visitors who do not read the language.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: The noimageindex rule tells Google not to index any of the images on the page, and John Mueller said he could not see why a site would want that.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: The unavailable_after rule lets a page drop out of search results after a set date and time, which suits time-bound pages, though John Mueller said most sites do not use it.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification says Googlebot considerably decreases the crawl rate of a URL after the date and time set in its unavailable_after rule.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: John Mueller's slide said Search Console has very few indexing-like settings and listed the Search generative AI control as the one control in his talk that is not a meta tag.
quote: Very few "indexing-like" settings are in Search Console

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: Setting the Search generative AI control in Search Console to exclude keeps a site's links and content out of Search generative AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode, so the site gets no traffic or impressions from them; include is the default.

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: To be as visible as possible in Google, John Mueller's closing slide recommended the robots rules max-image-preview:large and max-snippet:-1.
quote: To be as visible as possible in Google, use: max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Set max-snippet:-1 and max-image-preview:large on every indexable template unless licensing requires otherwise, and check that no CMS, plug-in or CDN setting adds lower snippet or image preview limits by default.

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: A slide said robots meta rules can be added to a page's HTML with JavaScript, but doing so takes more time.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's meta tags documentation recommends avoiding JavaScript to inject or change meta tags whenever possible and testing the implementation thoroughly when it must be used.

sources.title: meta tags and attributes that Google supports

speaker: John Mueller
label: slide
text: Removing a robots restriction such as noindex with JavaScript does not work, a slide said.
quote: But... it takes more time, and removing restrictions (like "noindex") doesn't work.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Ship robots rules in the HTML the server sends and never rely on JavaScript to lift a noindex: Google may skip rendering a page that arrives with noindex, so the page can stay out of the index even if a script removes the tag later.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller said robots meta rules only work if robots.txt allows Google to fetch the page.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: When robots.txt blocks a page, the page's content is not indexable but Google can still index its URL, John Mueller said.

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: When Google finds a noindex rule in a page's HTML, it drops the page without even processing its JavaScript, so a script cannot switch the page back to indexable, John Mueller said.
quote: we will see the noindex and say, oh, we will get rid of this page; we won't even process the JavaScript

speaker: John Mueller
label: stage
text: John Mueller recommended putting robots meta tags directly in a page's HTML exactly as intended, and adding them with JavaScript only where that is not possible, as in a JavaScript web app.

sources.title: meta tags and attributes that Google supports

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says that when Google encounters a noindex rule it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution, so using JavaScript to change or remove a noindex robots meta tag may not work as expected.
quote: it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: On stage the rule was absolute (Google won't even process the JavaScript of a page served with noindex), while Google's guide says only that it may skip rendering; either way, a noindex in the served HTML must never be one that JavaScript is expected to lift.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Google framed rendering historically: when Google started, most of the web was plain, semantic HTML it could extract directly, but the modern web is built with JavaScript and much content is generated by JavaScript, so Google had to adapt.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Without its ability to render JavaScript, Google says it would not be able to see most of what is on the web today.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: slide
text: Google renders pages in order to index what users see: its commitment to reflecting the user experience means understanding what people see when a page loads in a browser and surfacing that in Search.
quote: Rendering Pages to Index What Users See

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Compared with other search engines and AI crawlers, Google said its effort to mimic what the user sees is essential to keeping its knowledge of the web up to date and comprehensive; it did not say what the others do.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Being able to render and read JavaScript matters whether the client fetching a page is a search crawler or an AI system, Google said.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Google described the mission of its rendering as simply executing JavaScript, while the implementation is complex, expensive and difficult.
quote: our mission is very simple these days: execute JavaScript

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on top of Search results: they are a different experience of the same content Google already has.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: AI Overviews and AI Mode typically do not ground their answers by reading pages live, unlike Gemini when a user asks about a specific page, Google said.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: To train Gemini models, Google renders every page just as it does for Search, so a page that renders correctly for Search also works for Gemini training, provided the site allows its content to be used for training.
quote: if it works for Search, it works for Gemini for training

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: If Gemini training reuses the rendering done for Search, a site needs no separate rendering work for Gemini; whether its rendered content is used for training is decided with the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, not by rendering choices.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: When a Gemini user asks about a specific web page (for example, whether it says anything about the ruby HTML tag), the page is read at that moment rather than during crawling and may be used to ground the answer, which takes extra time.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawler documentation defines grounding in Gemini Apps and in Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI as providing content from the Google Search index to the model at prompt time, and sites manage whether their content is used for it with the Google-Extended robots.txt token.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google
label: docs
text: Google says user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a URL because a user asked for it in a Google product (for example Gemini Notebook fetching URLs users add as sources, or Google-Agent acting on a user's request), generally ignore robots.txt rules.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google documents Gemini grounding only as content from the Search index at prompt time; the live read of a specific page at a user's request, described on stage, is not documented, so it is unclear whether it works like a user-triggered fetcher, which generally ignores robots.txt, or follows Google-Extended.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Google's simple solution for the extra time of live page reads is to make JavaScript-generated content render quickly and efficiently, or to use server-side rendering.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: For pages people are likely to ask an AI assistant about (product, pricing, documentation and policy pages), server-render the main content so a live, user-triggered read does not depend on client-side JavaScript finishing quickly.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Google renders pages with Chromium, the browser technology that also underlies Chrome, Edge and other Chromium-based browsers.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: slide
text: A Google pipeline diagram ran from the crawl queue to the crawler, then through HTML parsing to processing, which passes pages to rendering and gets them back, and then to the index; rendering fetches its JavaScript and CSS through the crawler.

sources.title: Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling
Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Although Google's pipeline diagram shows rendering as part of indexing, Google's rendering is a detached system, kept separate because rendering is time-consuming and computationally expensive.
quote: it shows rendering as part of indexing, but it's actually a detached system

sources.title: Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: After the crawler has fetched a page, Google's rendering system executes it, checks that it loads properly and works out what it looks like at different sizes.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Google said its pipeline needs to ensure that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering, while content that appears only through JavaScript and CSS takes a longer rendering pass.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The stage remark that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering does not mean such pages skip rendering, because Google's guide queues every 200 page for rendering; read it as: content already in the raw HTML does not depend on the slower rendering pass.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Put everything indexing depends on (title, meta description, canonical, robots meta tag, main text and links) in the raw HTML so it is available without rendering, let JavaScript add enhancements only, and check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection for the rest.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: Google urged sites to make sure their JavaScript content can be crawled, rendered and indexed, calling this important today and also tomorrow, as AI systems increasingly ground answers to user requests.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Erin Sparling
label: stage
text: After Google's opener, Lightning session D had three community talks: rendering and JavaScript execution blind spots (Sören Bendig), debugging JavaScript rendering for Search (Rebecca Yu) and virtualizing the browser (Natalia Venditto).

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Many SEOs still treat everything beyond the raw HTML as the developers' business, but developers often do not handle rendering problems, a community speaker warned.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: slide
text: The first rendering blind spot a community speaker showed was content changes: text, images and recommendations that differ between the raw HTML and the rendered page, illustrated by a shop page whose rendered version had a whole extra section.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Switching JavaScript off and on in the browser gives a quick first impression of which content on a page depends on rendering.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: A community speaker strongly advised putting everything you want cited into the raw, server-side rendered HTML, especially for AI systems that cannot render JavaScript yet.
quote: everything you want cited, include it in the raw HTML, server-side rendered

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: In a navigation example, the main navigation was in the raw HTML and would survive a rendering failure, but the whole sub-navigation was built by JavaScript, so all of its links would be inaccessible to bots if rendering broke.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: When checking which links bots can see, keep in mind that the rendered HTML can change with user actions, a community speaker cautioned.

sources.title: Pagination, incremental page loading, and their impact on Google Search

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: One site that builds its whole content by rendering also rendered its meta description with HTML tags inside it, which makes no sense and points to a flawed process.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Sites that create their content by rendering should have at least basic monitoring to check that the rendered pages come out right, a community speaker advised.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Browser console messages reveal further problems on a page, Content Security Policy violations among them; few teams analyse console messages at scale, but they should, a community speaker said.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: On a travel site, the number of offers differed between the raw HTML and the rendered page, possibly because the two versions drew on different internal databases or applied extra filters.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: On a retail brand's page, the rendered version promised a bigger discount for a newsletter sign-up than the non-rendered version that was served, a mismatch that can hurt customer satisfaction; the two recordings disagree on the figure the rendered page promised.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Offer counts, discounts and other data should always be the same in the raw HTML and the rendered page, a community speaker advised.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Diff the raw and the rendered HTML of each key template for prices, offer counts, links and meta tags, and treat any difference in commercial data as a bug, because bots and users may get different versions.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: A search engine's renderer does not wait forever before taking its snapshot, so content from slow internal systems or APIs can be missing and unresolved placeholders can end up in the final snapshot, a community speaker said.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: In one shop's example, brand names and product descriptions were rendered from a database; the brand name was missing from the meta description, and the shop sometimes appeared with unresolved placeholders and sometimes as intended.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Unresolved placeholders caused by rendering timeouts are hard to catch because the problem moves around: it is not always the same page that is broken.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Broken titles and snippets caused by unresolved placeholders may hurt business, especially for e-commerce shops and affiliate-heavy sites, a community speaker warned.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: To catch intermittent rendering problems, archive the full HTML and the resources of each page during a site audit and analyse them yourself, a community speaker advised.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Add a check for unresolved template placeholders (such as {{brand}}, undefined or null) in rendered titles, meta descriptions and visible text to recurring crawls, and render the same URLs more than once, because such failures are intermittent.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Content Security Policy lowers the risk of cross-site scripting and clickjacking by defining trusted hosts; a resource from a host that is not trusted is not used.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Content Security Policy is often misunderstood: on a page of a large German banking group, a video that should have been shown was blocked by a CSP violation, which also appeared in the browser console.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Never block a resource that a page needs for rendering with robots.txt, a community speaker said, calling this common sense.

sources.title: Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: When something is missing from a rendered page, check both robots.txt and the Content Security Policy: the URL Inspection live test shows the page resources, the JavaScript console output and a screenshot of the rendered page.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: A page can render completely blank while its raw HTML looks fine, so a team checking only the raw HTML thinks all is well; causes include server misconfiguration, overload and bad scripts.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: slide
text: A community speaker summarised five rendering blind spots to check: content and markup changes, invisible links, rendering timeouts, Content Security Policy and blocked resources.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Because even established brands have these rendering problems and every modern website uses a lot of JavaScript, a community speaker argued that most sites probably have them too and that ignoring rendering is reckless.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: A community speaker strongly advised SEOs to use Chrome DevTools more often to understand what happens when their pages render.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Sören Bendig
label: stage
text: Third-party systems billed per session that also run when bots render a page can cost a high-traffic site thousands of euros per month, a community speaker said, adding that he sees this regularly.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google says Googlebot and its Web Rendering Service identify resources that do not contribute to essential page content, such as reporting and error requests, and may not fetch them, so client-side analytics may not give a full or accurate picture of their activity.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Compare the session counts that per-session-billed tools (chat, personalisation, testing, session replay) charge for with real user sessions, and load such tools only after a user interaction where they add no content that needs to be indexed.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: The second community lightning talk of the rendering block covered debugging JavaScript rendering for Search: how Google renders pages, a step-by-step check, four common mistakes and a worked product page example.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: The diagram from Google's JavaScript SEO basics page shows a URL going from the crawl queue to the crawler, the crawled HTML going to processing, then the render queue and the renderer, whose rendered HTML returns to processing before the page reaches the index.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: In Google's processing step, links are extracted from the HTML Google already has, before rendering, and the URLs found go back to the crawl queue.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable <a href> markup.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: After processing, an indexable page is placed in Google's render queue to wait for rendering.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: A community speaker's slide put the usual wait in Google's render queue at seconds to a couple of minutes per page.
quote: Usually from seconds to a couple minutes.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says a page may wait in the render queue for a few seconds but that it can take longer, and it gives no upper limit.
quote: The page may stay on this queue for a few seconds, but it can take longer than that.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: Google's renderer is a headless Chromium that runs the page's JavaScript.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Whatever is in the DOM at the moment Google's rendering finishes is what likely gets indexed.
quote: Whatever is in the DOM at that moment is what likely gets indexed.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: If a page keeps loading content indefinitely, not all of that content will be indexed, because Google's rendering does not go on forever (this passage of the recording is partly unclear).

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: To check whether JavaScript content is affected, open the URL Inspection tool in Search Console or the Rich Results Test and look for that content in the rendered HTML tab.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: A community speaker treats the rendered HTML shown in Google's testing tools as the final source of truth, because what Google sees there is what gets indexed.
quote: I always treat this page as the final source of truth

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Google's URL Inspection help says the tool's live test examines a URL in real time, so its results can differ from Google's indexed version of the page.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Check rendering per template rather than per URL: inspect one URL of each page type (product, category, article) in URL Inspection and confirm that the main content, prices and internal links appear in the rendered HTML.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: If content is missing from the rendered HTML, find the script responsible in Chrome DevTools: open the Network tab, filter by Fetch/XHR and reload the page.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: For each suspect script or API request in Chrome DevTools, check whether it runs, whether something blocks it and whether robots.txt disallows it.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: If the cause of missing JavaScript content is still unclear after checking the network requests, search the source code for a string related to the missing content.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: A community speaker listed four common but often overlooked JavaScript rendering mistakes: non-crawlable link markup, error pages that return HTTP 200 in single-page apps, content behind user interaction, and JavaScript or API resources blocked in robots.txt.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Google follows links in <a href> elements; a link that only runs an onclick handler, or a hash pseudo-link such as href=#/products, may be invisible to Google.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: The crawlable pattern for single-page app navigation is a real URL in the href, such as <a href=/products>, combined with History API routing (window.history.pushState) instead of hash routes.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: Non-crawlable link markup, such as onclick links and hash pseudo-links, is common in single-page web apps, and sites that use faceted navigation should check their links for it.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: A market or language selector built as a button works for users but leaves the whole cluster of alternate-language pages without crawlable links, so the cluster is orphaned for Google.
quote: The nav works perfectly for users, and the entire alternate-language cluster is orphaned.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Hash-fragment links are a problem only where Google should follow them: product, category and language links need a real URL in an <a href>, while fragments can deliberately keep filter combinations out of the crawl, as Google's faceted navigation guide allows.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Build market and language selectors as plain <a href> links to each alternate URL, not buttons or script handlers; otherwise the language versions have no internal links and depend on sitemaps to be found, which is slow.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: In single-page apps, a missing page often shows a custom 404 page while the server returns HTTP 200, because the front-end router, not the server, handles the 404.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: The fix for a client-side soft 404 is to make a missing page end with a real HTTP 404 status code instead of 200.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: In a single-page app, let the server return 404 for unknown routes where possible; otherwise use one of the two client-side fixes Google documents for error views: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404, or a robots noindex added with JavaScript.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: stage
text: A community speaker called not hiding content behind user interaction the most important of the four JavaScript rendering mistakes.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Content that loads only after a user action such as a click or a scroll is not in the DOM while Google renders the page, so Google cannot index it.

sources.title: Mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: For rendering, what matters is whether content is present in the DOM, not whether it is visible on screen: hidden content can be indexed, absent content cannot.
quote: Not visible versus hidden. Present versus absent in the DOM.

sources.title: Mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Lazy loading triggered by a scroll event listener, such as window.addEventListener('scroll', loadMoreProducts), never runs for Googlebot because Googlebot does not scroll.
quote: Googlebot doesn't scroll. Never runs.

sources.title: March 2023 Google SEO office hours
sources.publisher: Google Search Central (SEO office hours transcript, March 2023)

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Lazy loading should be triggered by an Intersection Observer that watches a sentinel element instead of by a scroll event listener.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: An Intersection Observer fires when the observed element enters the viewport, and the viewport Google renders with is tall, so content lazy-loaded this way can load during rendering.
quote: Fires on viewport entry. Viewport is tall.

sources.title: March 2023 Google SEO office hours
sources.publisher: Google Search Central (SEO office hours transcript, March 2023)

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Google Search Central (SEO office hours transcript, March 2023)
label: docs
text: In Google's March 2023 SEO office hours, John Mueller said Google handles infinite scroll with viewport expansion, rendering a page like a very long phone, which is not very efficient and can miss content, so pagination links are strongly recommended.
quote: this is done through a technique called "viewport expansion", where we render a page like a very long phone.

sources.title: March 2023 Google SEO office hours
sources.publisher: Google Search Central (SEO office hours transcript, March 2023)

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Tab or accordion content fetched from an API only when a user clicks the tab, as in tab.onclick = () => fetch('/api/specs'), does not exist for Google until someone clicks.
quote: Doesn't exist until someone clicks

sources.title: Mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices
Pagination, incremental page loading, and their impact on Google Search

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Tab and accordion content should be in the DOM from the start and only hidden with CSS or the hidden attribute; Google indexes such hidden content.
quote: CSS-hidden is fine. Google indexes it.

sources.title: Mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Audit tabs, accordions and 'load more' lists for content fetched on click or scroll: put tab content in the initial DOM and hide it with CSS, trigger lazy loading with an Intersection Observer, and give long lists paginated URLs linked with <a href>.

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Blocking JavaScript or API resources in robots.txt is a classic rendering mistake: if Google's renderer cannot fetch a resource, it cannot run it.
quote: If the renderer can't fetch it, the renderer can't run it.

sources.title: Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling

session: Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript
speaker: Rebecca Yu
label: slide
text: Disallowing a script folder such as /static/js/ or a generic /api/ folder in robots.txt can block the endpoints that supply a page's content, leaving blank modules and missing content after rendering.

sources.title: Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process
Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling
