speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Version 20 of the Screaming Frog SEO Spider, released in May 2024, was the first that could connect the crawler to ChatGPT through custom JavaScript, which let SEOs rewrite image alt text at scale.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: In a community speaker's case, an LLM asked to write alt text for a product image of a veterinary anxiety medicine for cats described only what it could see, a cat and a veterinarian, and dropped the stress, anxiety and medical-treatment intent of the page.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: After shipping LLM-rewritten image alt text on a client's site, a community speaker saw the site's image performance in Google Search Console drop (no figures were given).

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: To test LLM-generated alt text before a rollout, a community speaker recommended running the crawler's custom JavaScript in Screaming Frog's List mode on a few chosen URLs and reviewing the generated alt text, instead of crawling the whole site in Spider mode.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: Because not every generated alt text can be checked by hand, a community speaker's safer script adds the page title to the LLM's image description, so the alt text carries the page's intent and not only what the image shows.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker named the limits of the title-based alt-text script: it rewrites only the hero image, assumes the page title states the user's intent, had been tested in only one language or market, and runs on the free Gemini model.

speaker: unknown
label: stage
text: A community speaker warned that articles still recommend rewriting alt text with AI, called AI a tool, and said that adopting such new AI implementations without applying existing SEO knowledge can damage ranking performance.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: A community talk described 'prompt journalism' as journalistic and content work, such as interviews and podcasts, done with a prompt-assisted workflow whose aim is to optimize material already recorded, which holds expertise, quotes and context, rather than to create more content.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: The first step of a community speaker's prompt-assisted workflow is cleaning the interview transcript of fillers, a step that needs editorial and SEO judgment because a published page is read by many systems whose way of consuming it is unknown.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: A community speaker cited W3C guidance that, when cleaning a transcript, it is usually not appropriate to correct the speaker's grammar or other mistakes.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: In the mapping step of a prompt-assisted workflow, an AI system splits an interview transcript into chapters with timestamps, headings and entities; in a community speaker's example it correctly extracted the subsea cables 2Africa and Equiano from a passage on Internet infrastructure in Africa.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: A community speaker said the chapters and entities extracted from an interview transcript can then be used to generate metadata and structured data for the published content.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: The second step of the prompt-assisted workflow applies the newsroom's inverted pyramid (the five Ws and H first, then attribution and quotes, context and secondary text); because it is a fixed structure, it can be written as a prompt that generates the article.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: From one unified interview transcript, a community speaker's workflow produces a full article for the website and shorter angles for LinkedIn, Substack, X and YouTube.

speaker: Patrick Domanico
label: stage
text: A community speaker said publishers can also verify their social accounts in Search Console, which makes it easier to track the performance of content repurposed for social platforms.

sources.title: Analyze your social and video platform content performance in Search Console

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google may find a site's different language versions on its own, without the site owner doing anything, but owners can take steps to make this easier for Google.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Each language version should have its own URL; switching languages with cookies or by updating the content in place makes the versions very difficult for Google to handle.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang.

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: Language versions can also be language-plus-region variants: Google's example site had a generic English page (en), a UK English page (en-gb) and a Spanish page (es), each on its own URL.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's hreflang guide says language-specific subdomains such as en, en-gb or de in a URL are not used to determine a page's target audience; site owners must map the audience explicitly, for example with hreflang.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: Google's hreflang example lists every language version in the page's HTML head as a link element with rel=alternate, the version's full URL and its hreflang code (en, en-gb, es), including the page's own URL.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: Missing return links are a common hreflang mistake: if page X names page Y as a language version, page Y must link back to page X.
quote: If page X links to page Y, page Y must link back to page X.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Each page in an hreflang set must also list its own URL, and a missing self-reference is a common mistake Google sees.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: When the HTML head is not suitable for a page, hreflang can be given by other methods instead, such as listing the language versions in a sitemap.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Any one hreflang method is fine, but a site should use only one: Google often sees sites using two or three methods at the same time, with annotations that conflict.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's hreflang guide says its three methods (link elements in the HTML head, an HTTP Link header, which suits non-HTML files such as PDFs, and an XML sitemap) are equivalent; using several at once is allowed but brings no benefit in Search and is harder to manage.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google ignores hreflang annotations that point only one way, where page A names page B as a language version but page B does not name page A back.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's hreflang guide says a site that finds it hard to keep every language pair bidirectional may omit some languages on some pages, because Google still processes the pairs that point to each other; new language versions should at least link both ways with the original or dominant language.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google requires hreflang return links because an alternate URL is a full URL that can be on any domain, so without them any site could declare itself a language version of someone else's website.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's hreflang guide says alternate URLs must be fully qualified, including the protocol (https://example.com/foo, not //example.com/foo or /foo), and need not be on the same domain.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Audit hreflang per cluster rather than per page: check that every page lists itself and all its alternates, that every alternate links back, and that only one method (HTML head, HTTP header or sitemap) supplies the annotations.

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: hreflang language codes must be ISO 639-1 codes: Google's list of common mistakes marked se, dk and cz (the country codes of Sweden, Denmark and Czechia) as wrong and sv, da and cs (Swedish, Danish, Czech) as right.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Swedish content for Sweden is marked sv-SE, not se-SE: the language part must be the Swedish language code sv, even though Sweden's country code is SE.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Site owners do not need to memorise hreflang language and region codes, but should double-check every code when implementing hreflang.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Czech is a frequent hreflang error: CZ is the country code and ccTLD of Czechia, but the language code for Czech is cs.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: hreflang region codes must be ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 country codes; frequent mistakes are UK instead of GB for the United Kingdom, SW instead of CH for Switzerland and GE instead of DE for Germany.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: EU is not a valid hreflang region code: sites use it hoping to target the European Union, but hreflang targeting works only by country.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: Google also flagged LA used as a region code for Los Angeles (a city, not a country) and SA used for South Africa as wrong hreflang region codes.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: slide
text: A region code cannot be used on its own in hreflang: en and en-GB are valid values, but GB alone is not, because the value must name a language.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Validate hreflang values against the ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 lists in a crawler rule or build check rather than by eye: reserved codes such as UK and EU are simply ignored, but some plausible mistakes are valid codes for something else (se is Northern Sami, GE Georgia, LA Laos, SA Saudi Arabia) and silently point the annotation at the wrong audience.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google does not use hreflang to determine a page's language when indexing the page.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google determines a page's language for indexing from the page content, not from a language code in the URL.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google annotates each page with only one language in the index.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Pages that mix several languages make it very hard for Google to decide which language a page is in, so each page should make its target language obvious and avoid mixing languages.

sources.title: How Google knows what language to show in search results

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Scattered boilerplate in a second language is sometimes fine but still not recommended, partly because mixed languages on one page are odd for users.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's hreflang guide says pages that translate only the template (navigation, footer) around main content in one language still count as duplicates, because localized versions are duplicates only if the main content stays untranslated; it recommends hreflang for such pages.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Because Google reads a page's language from its content and stores one language per page, translate templates (navigation, footer, buttons, legal notices) together with the main text; large untranslated blocks risk the page being annotated with the wrong language.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The ccTLD (country-code top-level domain) is one of the most important and strongest signals Google uses to decide which country a site targets; Google also considers other signals, which matter less.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Server location is not really a reliable country-targeting signal nowadays, so Google does not use it much; the recording is unclear on the word 'server'.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: At the point where one recording names the ccTLD as the most important country-targeting signal, a second attendee recording heard 'IP address' instead; Google's multi-regional sites documentation names the ccTLD as a strong signal of a site's target country and server location only as a possible, not definitive one, so the ccTLD is the better-supported reading.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's documentation calls a ccTLD a strong signal that a site is meant for a certain country and still lists server location as a possible signal of a site's audience, though not a definitive one because sites use CDNs or are hosted abroad; it does not rank the signals.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: For country versions of a site, a ccTLD, subdomains or subdirectories are all acceptable choices; the right one depends on the site's needs, goals and resources.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's table of URL structures for country targeting gives pros and cons for a country-specific domain (example.de), a subdomain (de.example.com) and a subdirectory (example.com/de/) on a generic domain, and marks URL parameters (site.com?loc=de) as not recommended.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Of the URL structures for country versions in a table on Google's slide (not photographed), the speaker called only one a wrong choice: the last option, which the speaker did not name but said they really do not recommend.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: A separate ccTLD for each country version is not necessarily better, even though the ccTLD is one of the strongest country signals, and sites should not move their domain for that reason.
quote: Don't try to move your domain now.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Whether to use ccTLDs depends on whether the domain can be obtained, what it costs, local laws or regulations, and how committed the business is to expanding in that country.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: For a business testing new countries, subdirectories on the existing domain are usually the cheapest start; a ccTLD's stronger country signal pays off only where domain availability, cost, local rules and long-term commitment justify it, and an established domain should not be moved just for the signal.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google usually understands non-English words typed 'in English' (probably meaning romanised, Latin-letter spellings, which the speaker did not spell out); the speaker said this belongs to query interpretation, a Day 3 (serving) subject.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google usually understands a query word whether it is written with or without diacritics (accents).

sources.title: How search results may differ based on accented characters and interface languages

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Sites need no extra work to appear in AI Overviews and AI Mode: both work on top of the existing web results, so what works for web results also works for the AI features.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In classic results users can usually tell when content in their language is missing, poorly translated or from another country, but AI answers synthesize many sources and hide this; the speaker called it an invisible gap.
quote: an invisible gap

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Users often assume AI is all-knowing and borderless, but AI is still language-dependent: if an AI answer is synthesized from the top results, a query in another language draws on a totally different set of data.
quote: AI is still language-dependent

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
How Google knows what language to show in search results

author: Google Search Help
label: docs
text: Google's Search Help says the language a query is typed in is an important factor in choosing the language of results, alongside interface and device language, location and site owners' annotations, and that Google may also show results in other languages when they are helpful or when there is not enough information in the query's language.

sources.title: How Google knows what language to show in search results

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In the speaker's own experience, the differences between languages are larger in AI answers than in classic search results.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Site owners may want to research whether they show up in AI answers in each language and market they serve, to find blind spots.

sources.title: Introducing Search Generative AI performance reports in Search Console

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Check AI Overviews and AI Mode with native-language queries in each target market, not with translated English keywords, and compare with the country breakdown of Search Console's generative AI performance report; topics where competitors are cited and you are not point to missing or weak local content.

sources.title: Introducing Search Generative AI performance reports in Search Console

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Whether machine-translated content is acceptable depends on the case and is the site owner's decision, after weighing three things machine translation can miss: translation quality, local conventions and cultural adaptation.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: To show uneven machine-translation quality, the speaker showed Google Translate output of attendee questions from a visit to China with a Google colleague, Gary, some clear and some unintelligible, and a restaurant menu whose English listed an item called 'aggressive element'.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Localisation should account for local conventions such as date formats, which differ between Europe, the UK, the US and other countries, and calendars (in Thailand the current year is 2569), or a date can point users to the wrong day.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Treat machine translation as a first draft: have a native speaker review it and adapt dates, calendars and units before publishing, because unreviewed bulk translation that adds little value can also fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: According to the speaker, shoppers in Europe and the US pay a lot of attention to promotions and discounts when deciding to buy (no source for this was captured), one of the cultural factors localisation should take into account.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), US consumers judge product quality more by user feedback and reviews, while European shoppers seem to look more at brand reputation.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), German shoppers also rely heavily on expert recommendations and certifications when judging product quality.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), French shoppers particularly want to know where a product comes from.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Localise the trust signals on product pages, not only the words: if the findings shown hold for your category, lead with reviews in the US, brand reputation elsewhere in Europe, expert certifications in Germany and origin information in France, and test the order per market.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's hreflang guide says the ISO 639-1 language code can be followed by a script in ISO 15924 format, such as zh-Hant or zh-Hans, and by an optional ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 region code, as in zh-Hans-US.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said that working out a site's localized pages and which countries it targets is one of the difficult, complex tasks for it in indexing.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said incorrect hreflang language or region codes are a mistake it finds very often, with the same wrong codes coming up again and again, especially in Europe, because site owners assume the codes are easy.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: In a community speaker's audit case, a premium multifunctional-furniture maker about to be acquired had multilingual sites with clean translations by native speakers and hreflang tags that were in fairly good shape.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: In the same furniture-maker audit, the Dutch site had only a fraction of the conversions of the brand's other language sites, although it showed the same catalogue, the same hero products and the same photography.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: Checking a competitor during the furniture-maker audit, a community speaker found that a large furniture retailer's French and Dutch sites differ a little in the products they show and especially in their photography, with items apparently shown in much smaller rooms on the Dutch site.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker said her first guess, that Dutch homes are smaller than French ones, was wrong: Dutch and French homes have about the same floor area per person, and what differs is the type of house.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker said about 19% of homes in Europe are terraced houses on several floors, against 58% in the Netherlands; the matching Eurostat figures are 2019 shares of the EU and Dutch population living in semi-detached or terraced houses, not shares of homes.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: In a community speaker's comparison, a typical Dutch home is narrow and spread over several levels, often with very steep, narrow staircases that make furniture harder to install upstairs, while a typical French home has a wide ground floor and usually wide stairs.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: The lesson of the furniture-maker case was that the translation was correct but the target region had never been checked.
quote: the translation was right, but the region was never checked

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: When translations and hreflang are clean but one country version converts far worse, compare that market's product range, photography and delivery or installation constraints with local competitors before changing anything technical.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker framed international SEO around three signals to settle before working on hreflang: language (what people can read), region (who the content is for) and authority (why local people should trust the site).

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker said language versions need adjusting for regional variants of one language: 90 is 'quatre-vingt-dix' in France but 'nonante' in Belgium, and Swiss German differs from German, for example in whether the letter ß (Eszett) is used.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's documentation recommends hreflang annotations even when a site's versions differ only by small regional variations within one language, for example English-language content targeted to the US, GB and Ireland.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: Settling the region means deciding who the content is actually for, which shapes how the catalogue is organised, how prices look and which payment options each market gets.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: Of language, region and authority, a community speaker called language easy to settle and region solvable with a little research, while authority (why local people should trust a brand) has to be earned and built over time.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker stressed that an hreflang annotation for a country (her example was German for Austria, de-AT) does not by itself make a site established or trusted in that country; local authority has to be worked for.

sources.title: Tell Google about localized versions of your page

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's documentation lists the signals it uses to decide which locale a page targets: ccTLDs, hreflang statements, server location, and other signals such as local addresses and phone numbers, local language and currency, links from other local sites and Business Profile signals.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker cited a Semrush study that found at least one hreflang error on 75% of multilingual websites; the study, reported in February 2017, audited 20,000 sites with several language versions (the speaker recalled it as about five years old).

sources.title: 75% of Multilingual Websites Have Hreflang Implementation Mistakes

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker said the SEO industry has treated hreflang as the hard part of international SEO; hreflang is complicated, but the real hard part is the homework of understanding consumers in each market.
quote: the hard part is actually doing the homework to understand your consumers

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker said the answers about what consumers in each market want expire, because regional differences change over time.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: A community speaker showed a chart of search interest over time for ceiling fans in northern versus southern Europe, saying southern Europeans commonly have them at home while northern Europeans paid them no attention until the previous summer's heat waves (the talk was on 1 October 2026).

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Re-check regional demand for core product categories at least once a year, for example by comparing regions and seasons in Google Trends, because climate, housing or habits can shift what a market wants.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: The first of three questions to ask before the technical work of international SEO is which languages, and which language variants, the site actually serves, keeping languages and variants apart.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: The second question before international SEO work is what genuinely differs between the regions of each language, such as photography, content, vocabulary, the way products are presented, pricing, catalogues and payment options.

speaker: Alizée Baudez
label: stage
text: The third question is whether you can name three local sources that already treat the brand as present in a country; if you cannot, a community speaker advised not to expand there but to fix the markets you already serve.
quote: don't bother expanding to another country; just fix the ones you already have

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Treat hreflang as a way to show the right language version, not as a market-entry signal: before launching a country version, make sure local publications, partners or directories already mention the brand, and localise pricing and payment options.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: List language variants such as fr-FR and fr-BE or de-DE and de-CH separately in a site's language inventory, and give each its own vocabulary and spelling review instead of reusing one translation for every country.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: A community talk, presented on its author's behalf by a colleague, was about multilingual SEO for languages written in non-Latin scripts, such as Persian and Arabic.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Arabic and Persian contain letters that look identical to users but are different characters to software, with different Unicode code points; the example given was the letter ye, which has an Arabic and a Persian form.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Because Arabic and Persian lookalike letters have different code points, a searcher may type one variant of a word while a website's text uses the other.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Lookalike Arabic and Persian character variants cause problems for data analysis and keyword research: data for one term can be split across the variants, which makes keyword research less accurate.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: For Persian and Arabic keyword research, look up each lookalike-character spelling of a term separately and add up the volumes, and check which variant the site's own content uses.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Persian and Arabic are written right to left and English left to right, so a title that mixes the two scripts can display in a confusing, unpredictable order even when its content is correct.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: The display problem of mixing right-to-left and left-to-right text also affects product titles and URLs, the presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said, showing an example from a large Iranian e-commerce site.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Users of non-Latin-script languages do not always search in their own script: the same Persian query may be typed in Persian script or in Latin letters, with the same intent and the same expected results.

sources.title: How Google Search handles multilingual searches

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Keyword research for non-Latin-script languages should ask how people actually type and spell in local search, not only what the right keyword is, because switching keyboards is inconvenient, especially when typing on mobile.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said that in competitive Persian, Turkish and Arabic searches, bought backlinks and paid editorial content still visibly influence rankings and are widespread (an observation; no data was shown); the presenter stressed this described the situation and was not a recommendation.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said Google announced in October 2023 that it had improved its spam-detection coverage for languages: the spam policy was global, but the coverage improvement was language-specific.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said Persian offers far fewer natural link opportunities than English, with fewer publications, niche blogs and websites.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: For SEO in languages such as Persian, the presenter of the non-Latin-script talk advised accepting different competitive dynamics and basing strategy on the actual maturity of that language's market, not only on the global policy.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: Google search features often launch in some languages or countries first and expand later (the presenter's example was site names, launched in several languages and then extended to all languages in 2023), so comparisons of performance across languages and countries should not assume a feature is live everywhere at once.

sources.title: Site names on Google Search now available for all languages

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: In the presenter's observation, AI answers to Persian queries are written in Persian but cite some English sources; the presenter explained that Persian content on a topic is often thinner, of lower quality or less relevant, so the systems retrieve from languages with better content, which the presenter called cross-lingual retrieval.

sources.title: How Google Search handles multilingual searches

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: The non-Latin-script talk concluded that multilingual SEO is not just translation: script, language behaviour and market maturity also matter, and basic SEO tactics, though the same everywhere, must be fitted to each market.

speaker: a second community speaker
label: stage
text: The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk recalled that Google officially treats buying links for ranking as spam (the year of the announcement was not clear in the recording).

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

author: Search Central blog (4 October 2023)
label: docs
text: Google's October 2023 spam update post (4 October 2023) says the update improved coverage in many languages and spam types, cleaning up spam reported in Turkish, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Hindi, Chinese and other languages, particularly cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The October 2023 spam update cited in the non-Latin-script talk names neither Persian nor Arabic (only 'other languages') and lists cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam, not link spam, so it does not show that the bought links the presenter saw working in Persian or Arabic search were addressed.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

author: Search Central blog (7 September 2023)
label: docs
text: Google's site names were introduced on mobile results for select languages in October 2022, expanded to desktop in March 2023, and on 7 September 2023 became available in all languages where Google Search is available, on mobile and desktop.

sources.title: Site names on Google Search now available for all languages

author: Search Central blog (8 September 2023)
label: docs
text: Google's post on multilingual searches (8 September 2023) says that, because of typing difficulty on some keyboards, a person in India might search in Hindi using Latin rather than Devanagari characters and want and receive Hindi results written either way.

sources.title: How Google Search handles multilingual searches

speaker: Community speakers
label: stage
text: Google added a poster session to the Deep Dive because some topics need a longer, more one-to-one discussion than a seven-minute lightning talk allows.

speaker: Community speakers
label: stage
text: The Day 2 poster topics included technical SEO testing in CI/CD pipelines, internal links that move rankings, Search Console's URL Inspection tool and API, getting everyone on board during complex site migrations, a CMS migration from WordPress to Contentful, the 'global Spanish' problem and going beyond prompts.

speaker: Community speakers
label: stage
text: One Day 2 poster was presented by a Googler, about bringing Google's tools into WordPress sites.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Among the many signals Google calculates during indexing, the ones singled out as having large effects on search results were country, language, freshness, SafeSearch and spam.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Country and language are among Google's most important signals and have been used since Google's early days.
quote: Both of them are extremely, extremely important

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Smaller languages have fewer documents on the web and so worse coverage, from an indexing perspective, than large ones, for example Basque compared with Spanish or Portuguese, Hungarian compared with German, and Sicilian compared with Italian.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google detects the language of each document and weights language in index selection so that the index is not dominated by one or two languages.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Without language or country input to index selection, Google's index would become an English index, because so many documents on the web are in English.
quote: if you just let the index decide what to rank without language or country input, then you would have an English index

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google also takes country into account in index selection, so that countries producing less content in a shared language, such as the UK for English or Switzerland for German, are not disadvantaged against the US or Germany, which produce most of it.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In ranking, country and language signals help Google serve users the right content for their country and language.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: A site serving a smaller country in a big language, such as British English or Swiss German, should make that country unmistakable (country-code domain or region-specific hreflang, local address, prices and currency) so its pages can benefit from index selection's country balancing instead of competing with the much larger US or German content pool.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Freshness is a signal for queries that deserve fresh results ('query deserves freshness'): when a breaking event hits a city, such as possible closure of Barcelona's airport, users want really fresh results, not results from two weeks ago.

sources.title: A guide to Google Search ranking systems

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google calculates some freshness signals during indexing but uses them in ranking.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
A guide to Google Search ranking systems

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Freshness plays no big role in index selection: whether a page was published 30 years ago or today makes no difference to its chance of being indexed.
quote: It doesn't play a big role in index selection.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Changing a page's date or making cosmetic edits will not help an old page get indexed, because freshness plays no big role in index selection; freshness pays off only when ranking for queries that deserve fresh results.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google uses multiple systems to protect users from unexpected explicit results: its algorithms detect whether a user is looking for explicit content and rank results accordingly, so the aim is not to never show explicit results but to avoid showing them to users who are not looking for them.

sources.title: Guidelines for sites with explicit content

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Whether a page's content is explicit does not matter for indexing: judged on content type alone, an explicit page has the same chance of being indexed as a major news site's homepage.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google calculates SafeSearch signals during indexing rather than in ranking, because ranking happens online with no time for such calculations, while indexing has the processing power.
quote: In ranking, everything has to happen online, and there's just not enough time to calculate those things.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Calculating SafeSearch signals for a page needs its whole parsed HTML plus knowledge of which pages link to it and which pages it links to.

sources.title: Guidelines for sites with explicit content

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's guidelines for sites with explicit content recommend grouping explicit pages on a separate domain or subdomain; otherwise Google's systems may judge the whole site explicit and filter all of it when SafeSearch is on.

sources.title: Guidelines for sites with explicit content

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Because explicit content on its own does not lower a page's chance of being indexed, the practical risk for a site that mixes explicit and general content is SafeSearch classification, which looks at the whole page and its links; keep explicit pages on a separate domain or subdomain, as Google advises.

sources.title: Guidelines for sites with explicit content

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Spam stops a document at indexing: when Google detects that a document is spam, it does not let it into the index.
quote: If we detect that something is spam, then we're not letting it into the index.

sources.title: How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's spam policies say that sites violating them may rank lower in results or not appear in results at all.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google uses more and more AI to detect spam, and Google's testing shows that this AI-based detection is highly accurate.

sources.title: Google Search spam updates and your site
How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: SpamBrain, Google's AI-based spam detection system, is nowadays built on Gemini and fine-tuned specifically for finding spam.
quote: built on top of, well, nowadays, Gemini, and fine-tuned to that specific purpose of finding spam

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: SpamBrain is central to Google's spam-fighting efforts and has been improved many times since its launch.

sources.title: How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022
How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021

author: Search Central blog (21 April 2022)
label: docs
text: Google's 2021 webspam report says SpamBrain, its AI-based spam-prevention system, was launched in 2018 and has been continuously improved since.

sources.title: How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The SpamBrain launch year mentioned on stage, with hesitation, was 2022, which does not match Google's documented 2018; 2022 is the year of the improvements described in Google's 2022 webspam report, so cite 2018 as the launch year.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: SpamBrain was said to detect 5 times more spam sites than the spam algorithms Google had launched before it.

author: Search Central blog (11 April 2023)
label: docs
text: Google's 2022 webspam report says SpamBrain detected 5 times more spam sites in 2022 than in 2021, and 200 times more than when it first launched.

sources.title: How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The '5 times more spam sites' figure said on stage matches Google's 2022 webspam report, but the report compares 2022 with 2021 (and gives 200 times since launch), not SpamBrain with earlier algorithms; quote the documented comparison.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google's testing shows that, thanks to SpamBrain, more than 99% of visits from Search are now spam-free.

sources.title: How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Language, country, SafeSearch and spam signals, and some freshness signals, are calculated when a page is indexed, so a fix such as correcting a page's language or removing content that triggers SafeSearch only counts once Google recrawls and reprocesses the page; request recrawling of the most important URLs after the fix.

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Many of Google's signals are described in its developer documentation, though not always under the name 'signals'.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
A guide to Google Search ranking systems

speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Combing Google's documentation for signals is not the best use of an SEO's time; creating content that users will like is a better one.
quote: If you are just focusing on actually creating the content that users will like, then that's probably a better use of your life.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's guidelines for sites with explicit content say to mark each explicit page with rating markup set to adult, either as a meta tag named rating or as an HTTP response header.

sources.title: Guidelines for sites with explicit content

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google's index is immense but finite, so Google cannot index every URL it finds on a web with a practically infinite number of URLs.
quote: our index is immense. Like, immense. But it is a finite resource.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google gives two reasons for not indexing every URL it knows: most of them would not be useful to users, and including URLs in the index that users would never see would be an immense investment.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google's index selection system calculates thresholds and decides which documents are kept and which are thrown out; a URL that does not meet the thresholds is not indexed.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection aims to index only documents that are useful to users now or potentially in the future.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection is a predictive AI system that relies heavily on machine learning.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection uses what Google already knows about a site: if the site, or even a section of it, satisfies users' needs well, new URLs from it are treated more forgivingly.
quote: the index selection system is going to be more forgiving when it sees a new URL from your site

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Launch new pages under sections that Google already indexes well, and improve or remove weak sections, because index selection judges new URLs partly by what it knows about the site and the section they sit in.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection uses the signals calculated earlier in indexing for each document it has to select or discard.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection is the last step before documents enter Google's index.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: When Google's coverage of a country is limited, index selection becomes more likely to select documents relevant to that country, even if other signals would suggest otherwise.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: When Google lacks content in a language, such as Basque, index selection becomes more likely to select lower-quality documents in that language.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Under-served languages were presented as an opportunity: where Google's index holds a lot of spam in a language such as Basque, a site that starts publishing in that language can very likely replace that spam with its own content and rank for those keywords (one clause of the reasoning was inaudible).

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The overall importance of a document or site plays a significant role in index selection.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: News sites were given as the example of importance at work in index selection: they are generally very important on the web and their pages usually get indexed very fast ('indexed' is a likely but not certain reading of the recording).

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Page quality is ultimately what decides whether a document is indexed, so focusing on quality is the most reliable way to get pages into Google's index.
quote: focusing on the quality is the most reliable way to get stuff in the index

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection applies the negative signals that immediately block indexing: noindex (the likely reading of one unclear word), expired unavailable_after dates, soft 404s, non-canonical duplicates, spam signals and other policies.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications
How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection drops a document carrying a noindex rule if it was not already dropped earlier in processing (noindex is a likely but not certain reading of the transcript, supported by the later mention of noindex among the Page indexing report reasons).

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection checks for the robots unavailable_after rule and its date, and drops a page from the index once that date is reached.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Use the unavailable_after robots rule on pages with a known end date, such as event pages, time-limited offers or job ads, so that index selection drops them automatically when the date passes instead of leaving expired pages in search results.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection drops soft 404 pages that were not dropped earlier, for example when a document is reprocessed.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: When Google already has duplicate information for a document, for example when reprocessing it, index selection uses it to drop non-canonical duplicates from further processing, so that, as the speaker put it, only canonicals end up in search results (a simplification; see D2-C703).

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's documentation says a search result usually points to the canonical page, but the other pages in a duplicate cluster are alternate versions that may be served in different contexts, for example a mobile page for a user on a mobile device.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: 'Only canonicals end up in search results' as said on stage is a simplification: non-canonical duplicates are dropped from the index, but Google's documentation says an alternate from the same cluster can still be shown in some contexts, such as a mobile version to a mobile user.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection loads most of Google's spam signals and acts as a gatekeeper so that no spam enters search results.
quote: index selection acts as a gatekeeper, ensuring that no spam enters our search results

sources.title: How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Index selection also applies other policies, covering egregious violations and, in a less certain reading of the transcript, content Google is legally not allowed to index.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: 'Discovered – currently not indexed' in Search Console is a crawl-scheduling state: Google knows the URL exists but does not want to crawl it yet. Of the two not-indexed statuses discussed, it was called the 'kind of nastier' one.
quote: The first one is kind of nastier.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Google's Page indexing report help says a 'Discovered – currently not indexed' page was found but not crawled yet, typically because Google wanted to crawl it but expected the crawl to overload the site, so it rescheduled the crawl.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The help page explains 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by expected server overload (capacity), while on stage it was explained as Google not wanting the URL yet (demand); the crawl budget guide covers both, so first rule out slow responses and server errors, then treat the status as a quality and demand problem.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Site owners can influence 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by getting other URLs of the site indexed and showing Google's systems that the site's content is good and useful to users.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Repeatedly submitting 'Discovered – currently not indexed' URLs does not change why they wait, because the status reflects a crawl-scheduling decision; raise the site's demonstrated quality instead, for example by improving or removing weak pages that are already indexed.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: 'Crawled – currently not indexed' in Search Console is an index selection decision: Google crawled and processed the page but decided not to keep it in the index.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Google's Page indexing report help says a 'Crawled – currently not indexed' page was crawled but not indexed, may or may not be indexed in the future, and does not need to be resubmitted for crawling.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: If content quality is even across a site, a page reported as 'Crawled – currently not indexed' may be using a different template that keeps Google from understanding where its content is.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is most of the time a quality issue rather than a technical one: the pages are usually low quality or useless for the index, for example duplicates or soft 404s.
quote: most of the time it is actually a quality issue

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The first thing to check for pages reported as 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is whether their quality is on par with the parts of the site that Google does index.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Treat 'Crawled – currently not indexed' as a quality audit list: compare those URLs with indexed pages of the same type for thin, duplicate or soft-404-like content and for template differences before looking for technical faults.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Search Console's Page indexing report is the place to check for index selection issues, and its not-indexed reasons are useful when testing changes on a site.

session: Deciding what goes in the index?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Not-indexed reasons in the Page indexing report include pages excluded by a noindex rule and 'Alternate page with proper canonical tag'.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The speaker recapped Google's pipeline up to the index: Google crawls pages, processes the fetched documents and then stores them in its index.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google's Search index stores the tokens produced by tokenizing each page, as they are, together with the metadata attached to the tokens during tokenization.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google's Search index does not hold the full content of pages; Google said storing full pages and pulling them out at serving time would be a very inefficient way of doing search.
quote: we don't have the full content of the page in our index

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Each document in Google's index has pretty much all the signals calculated for it attached, for example quality signals plus the page's country and language, according to an illustration the speaker called an approximation of the real structure.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: The snippet shown for a web result is reconstructed from the tokens stored in Google's index: Google knows the position of each token in the document and rebuilds the snippet from those positions.
quote: the snippet that you see was reconstructed from these tokens

session: How does the index look like?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's snippet documentation says snippets are created automatically, primarily from the page content, to preview the part that best relates to the user's specific search, so one page can get different snippets for different searches; sometimes the meta description is used instead.

sources.title: Control your snippets in search results

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same index structures and token-based snippets as classic web results, a point Google called important but not obvious.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said that when AI Overviews or AI Mode run a query fan-out, the generated queries are sent to Google's Search index and documents come back with their snippets, which then feed the AI-generated answer (part of this passage is unclear in the recording).

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: How does the index look like?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's robots meta tag specification says the nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode, and max-snippet also limits how much of it may be used that way.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: How does the index look like?
author: Google Search Central, Google blog (5 March 2025)
label: docs
text: Google says query fan-out in AI Overviews and AI Mode issues related searches across subtopics and several data sources, which for AI Mode include the Knowledge Graph and shopping data as well as web content (AI Mode launch post, March 2025).

sources.title: Expanding AI Overviews and introducing AI Mode

session: How does the index look like?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: There is no separate AI index to optimise for: when a page never shows up as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, first check that it is indexed, that no nosnippet rule blocks its snippet and that the site is not excluded in Search Console's generative AI setting, the eligibility conditions Google lists.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: How does the index look like?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.

sources.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: To find relevant pages, Google's serving system relies on posting lists, a long-established information retrieval structure taught in computer science courses, because simply asking for every page that contains a word would not work.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said posting lists, which Google's serving system uses to find the pages that contain a query's words, are not new: they are at least 60 years old (as of 2026).

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: For most of the tokens Google finds on the web, though not every single one, the index keeps a posting list of the URLs that contain that token.

session: How does the index look like?
author: Google Search (How Search Works)
label: docs
text: Google's How Search Works site describes the Search index as like the index at the back of a book, with an entry for every word seen on every webpage Google indexes.
quote: It’s like the index in the back of a book - with an entry for every word seen on every webpage we index.

session: How does the index look like?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The speaker's 'most of the tokens' is more precise than the public explainer's 'an entry for every word': the explainer simplifies, and the speaker's self-correction suggests some tokens get no posting list, though the speaker did not say which.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In posting-list retrieval, the posting lists of the query's words are intersected, which yields an unranked list of candidate URLs.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: A search query is broken into words with the same segmenter or tokenizer that Google used to build the index.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: At retrieval, Google looks up the posting lists of the query words that are actually important rather than of every word in the query.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Besides posting lists, Google can retrieve documents through vector embeddings: parts of documents are associated with embeddings, which form a vector space used for retrieval.
quote: just like you build a posting list, you can also build a vector space

sources.title: How AI powers great search results
A guide to Google Search ranking systems

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: In embedding-based retrieval, the distance between the embeddings of documents and the embedding of the user's query decides which documents are returned.

sources.title: How AI powers great search results
A guide to Google Search ranking systems

session: How does the index look like?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Write for both retrieval routes without keyword stuffing: name the page's subject in the plain words people search with, because posting lists match the words on the page, and explain the topic fully, because embedding retrieval matches meaning, so every keyword variation is unnecessary.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said a vector space also holds embeddings for associations the web makes with a page, such as what is known about its author; most of them sit far from typical queries, and a query that names the association may move closer to them.

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Both retrieval methods Google described, the long-established posting lists and the newer vector embeddings, work from the content of the page.

sources.title: How AI powers great search results

session: How does the index look like?
speaker: Google
label: stage
text: Google said, hedging with 'I think', that because retrieval is still based on content, the content mantra Google started about 25 years ago (as of 2026) still stands.
quote: this mantra that we started 25 years ago or whatever still stands, whether we like it or not

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends is a free Google tool that gives access to a sample of aggregated, anonymized and categorized searches.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends data covers searches on Google Search, including web, image, shopping and news search, plus searches on YouTube.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Discover is not included in Google Trends, because Discover is a content feed with no search box, while Trends counts only the queries people type into Google Search or YouTube.

author: Google Trends Help
label: docs
text: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends filters out searches made by Google products and services, including the internal searches made by AI Mode and AI Overviews.
quote: This includes internal searches made by AI Mode and AI Overviews.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google Trends cannot show demand that reaches people through the Discover feed, so Discover visibility has to be judged from Search Console's Discover performance report rather than from Trends.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google handles more than five trillion searches a year, a figure Google announced publicly at the beginning of 2025.

sources.title: AI, personalization and the future of shopping

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: By the author's arithmetic, more than five trillion Google searches a year means on average more than 13.7 billion searches a day, or roughly 160,000 a second.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends data can be viewed for the whole world, for a single country or for a region within a country, for example Spain or Catalonia.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google said Google Trends data is almost real time, reaching up to a few minutes before the moment of viewing.
quote: we have data that goes all the way back from 2004 and up until three minutes ago

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends offers time ranges from the past hour or the past day back to 2004, so search patterns can be compared across two decades.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google argued that people search authentically, for health conditions, career troubles or home repairs, so aggregated searches reflect what a country or the world cares about better than the curated picture on social media.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends has two flagship experiences: the Explore page and Trending now.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: The Google Trends Explore page, which Google called the heart of Trends, shows search interest in a query or topic and how it changes over time.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google launched a brand-new Google Trends Explore page at the beginning of 2026.

sources.title: An easier way to explore Search trends with Gemini

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: The legacy Google Trends Explore page is still available but will be retired: Google is adding its features to the new Explore page until everyone can move to the new one (no date was given).
quote: the legacy Explore page, which is still available, but not for a long time

author: Google Trends Help
label: docs
text: Google's Trends Help says Google Trends compares up to 8 groups of terms at once, with up to 50 terms in each group, while Classic explore (the legacy page) supports 5 groups of up to 25 terms.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Trending now, a tab at the top of Google Trends, shows the topics people are searching for on Google right now.

sources.title: Explore the searches that are Trending now

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google said Trends' Trending now covered 125 countries at the time of the talk (October 2026), plus regions within many of those countries.

sources.title: 3 Trending Now updates to help you keep up with the latest trends
Explore the searches that are Trending now

author: Google blog (14 August 2024), Google Trends Help
label: docs
text: Google's August 2024 blog post said Trending now was available in 125 countries, with regional trends in 40 of them; the current Trends Help page says 100+ countries and regions.

sources.title: 3 Trending Now updates to help you keep up with the latest trends
Explore the searches that are Trending now

author: Google Trends Help, Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's documentation says the Trending now page shows an approximate, bucketed search volume for each trend, with its growth against a predicted baseline.

sources.title: Explore the searches that are Trending now

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: A Google Trends Explore chart presented on stage put worldwide search interest in Gemini above ChatGPT for the first time ever in September 2025, during a sharp surge for Gemini.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google attributed the September 2025 surge in worldwide search interest for Gemini to the viral launch of Nano Banana (the image editing model in the Gemini app), as people searched for both Gemini and Nano Banana.

author: Google blog (26 August 2025)
label: docs
text: Google announced Nano Banana, a new image editing model from Google DeepMind in the Gemini app, on 26 August 2025.

sources.title: Image editing in Gemini just got a major upgrade

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: On stage the Nano Banana launch was placed in September 2025, but Google announced it on 26 August 2025, so the September 2025 surge in Gemini search interest described in the talk came in the weeks after the launch.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: After the Nano Banana surge faded, worldwide baseline search interest in Gemini stayed much higher than before, which Google read as a sustained gain in brand recognition.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Real-world events such as product launches show up directly in Google Trends search interest graphs.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: To judge a launch or campaign in Google Trends, compare the brand's baseline search interest before and after the spike, not only the height of the spike, because a lasting baseline lift is the durable gain.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: A Google Trends chart of worldwide search interest in AI from 2004 to mid-2025 showed a huge rise in the two to three years before mid-2025.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google said worldwide search interest in AI has climbed far higher since mid-2025, beyond the range of the 2004 to mid-2025 chart shown in the talk.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: An early-2012 worldwide spike in Google Trends search interest for 'ai' was caused by the global hit song 'Ai Se Eu Te Pego', whose title contains the Portuguese word 'ai', not by interest in artificial intelligence.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: A Google Trends engineer found the cause of the 2012 'ai' spike by zooming in on that time range on the Explore page and reading the related queries.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google advised being curious and digging deeper when explaining a pattern in Google Trends, because context matters and the obvious explanation is sometimes wrong.

author: Google Trends Help
label: docs
text: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends adds statistical noise to protect privacy, so one-off spikes on queries with low or no search interest may be noise rather than real search activity.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Before treating a spike in an ambiguous keyword as demand for your topic, zoom in on the period in Google Trends and check the commonly searched queries, since another meaning of the word (as with 'ai' in 2012) may be driving it.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski since 2004 shows strong seasonality, peaking every winter.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski also shows a mostly steady decline since 2004, which can be misread as falling search volume.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends shows search interest, not search volume: each point on its 0 to 100 scale represents the share of searches for the term out of all searches.
quote: Search interest is not search volume.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Because total Google searches were far fewer in 2004 than today, a falling search interest share in Google Trends can hide a rising number of searches.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google said its internal numbers show the actual volume of ski-related searches is going up, even though ski's share of all searches in Google Trends has declined since 2004.
quote: we can tell you from our own internal numbers that we're seeing on Google Trends: the actual volume is, in fact, going up.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google stressed that the difference between search interest and search volume matters most when reading very long time ranges in Google Trends.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: A Google Trends line that falls over many years is not proof that a market is shrinking; compare terms against each other in the same chart, and take absolute numbers from keyword tools or Search Console impressions.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google presented three uses of Google Trends for content creation, marketing and SEO: keyword selection, scheduling and ideation.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: For keyword selection, Google recommended entering candidate keywords on the Google Trends Explore page, setting the relevant country, region and time frame, and seeing which terms have the higher search interest.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google recommended using the keywords with higher search interest in Google Trends in page titles and marketing campaigns.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's Search Central guide to Google Trends says to use Trends to inform a content strategy only where a topic fits the business and its users, and to focus on terms where the site has expertise and experience.
quote: you shouldn't write about something just because it's trending

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Compare candidate keywords in Google Trends for the exact country or region where the page should rank, because the higher-interest wording can differ between markets that share a language.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: The 'Commonly searched queries' section of the new Google Trends Explore page, called related queries in the legacy Explore page, lists queries that people typed in the same search sessions as the entered term.

sources.title: Understanding How the Google Trends Explore Page uses Gemini models

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google Trends' commonly searched queries come as top queries, with the highest search interest or volume, and rising queries, with the largest increase from the previous time frame to the current one.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google recommended checking both the top and the rising commonly searched queries in Google Trends when selecting keywords.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: In Google Trends' commonly searched queries, rising queries point to emerging sub-topics worth a new page or section, while top queries show the established wording to reuse in titles and headings.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: For scheduling, Google recommended checking on the Google Trends Explore page whether the topics relevant to your domain show seasonality; many topics do, though not all.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Where a topic is seasonal in Google Trends, Google said the pattern predicts the next wave of search interest, which is the time to run a marketing campaign or have content ready.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: A Google Trends chart of US search interest over five years showed umbrella and sunscreen correlated, both peaking in June, against the common assumption that umbrella searches peak in winter.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
text: Google warned that assumptions about when search interest peaks are sometimes wrong, and advised checking the pattern in Google Trends for your own target market.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Publish or refresh seasonal content a few weeks before the seasonal rise that Google Trends shows for each target country, so the pages are crawled and indexed before demand peaks.

speaker: Omri Weisman
label: stage
