speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: slide
text: Google's talk 'Mastering the messy middle', given by a Google marketing research and insights manager, presented Google's research on how AI is changing the way consumers make purchase decisions.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google has used the 'messy middle' decision-making model since 2019; the messy middle is what happens between the trigger that starts a purchase journey and the purchase itself.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: In the messy middle people are in one of two mindsets: exploring, which looks across the category, its price points, its brands and what is available, or evaluating, which works toward a position where a decision can be made.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Shoppers loop back and forth between exploring and evaluating until they feel confident enough to commit to a purchase.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

author: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)
label: docs
text: Google's Think with Google report 'Marketing in the messy middle' places the messy middle between trigger and purchase and models it as two looping mindsets: exploration, an expansive mindset that adds brands, products and category information, and evaluation, a reductive mindset that narrows the options down to a decision.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

author: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)
label: docs
text: Google's messy-middle report cites its original Decoding Decisions study, run with The Behavioural Architects in the UK in 2019 with 31,000 in-market online shoppers and published in 2020; the report says the findings were validated in more than 20 countries.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's researcher explained the looping in the messy middle as a tension between people's urge to collect more information and the mental effort of processing it, a subject studied by behavioural science.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: How AI is changing decision making is the number one question Google's consumer insights team receives, according to the speaker in October 2026.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's research on how AI changes consumer purchase decisions, presented in October 2026, was based on 23,000 conversations with consumers (the talk did not say in which countries).

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Because people do not always do what they say they will do, Google's research on AI and purchase decisions also analysed panels with 40,000 participants, together with research partners, besides the consumer conversations (the talk did not make clear whether 40,000 is one panel or the total).

author: DMEXCO 2026 event programme
label: press
text: The DMEXCO 2026 programme described a Google session, 'Beyond the Messy Middle: Mastering the consumer journey with AI' (24 September 2026), as based on tens of thousands of AI-moderated interviews and observed journeys across Europe, finding that consumers are being 'boosted' by AI.

sources.title: Beyond the Messy Middle: Mastering the consumer journey with AI

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Keep the research numbers apart when quoting them: the 23,000 consumer conversations and 40,000-participant panels behind the 2026 AI findings are a newer research wave than the 2019 messy-middle study of 31,000 UK online shoppers.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's headline finding was that people who use AI features such as AI Mode or AI Overviews feel much more confident about their purchase decisions.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Behavioural science distinguishes a fast, emotional way of deciding, used for frequent low-stakes decisions, from a slow, effortful way used for high-stakes decisions, which is tiring.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's research found that consumers delegate the mental effort of a purchase decision to AI without surrendering the choice itself, which Google calls being 'boosted'.
quote: that doesn't mean they are surrendering their choices. What's happening is that consumers are feeling boosted.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: According to Google's research, AI turns consumers who were confused and overwhelmed by information and options into consumers who feel empowered, like category experts, and able to make the best purchase for their needs.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: The first benefit consumers get from AI, according to Google's research, is ease: AI synthesises information quickly into an easy-to-digest form and makes choice overload manageable, so consumers can offload cognitive effort.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's research also counted easy access as part of AI's ease benefit: multimodal input, such as taking pictures, and low friction lower the barrier to entry.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: The second benefit, assistance, is that AI reduces a complex category, such as smartphones or trip planning, to the few features that really matter (for a phone, the battery and the picture quality), so consumers feel like experts.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Assistance also includes showing consumers what people in similar situations chose, because people are social and want that reassurance (the wording of this passage is partly uncertain in the recording).

author: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)
label: docs
text: Google's messy-middle report names six behavioural principles at work in the messy middle: category heuristics, power of now, social proof, scarcity bias, authority bias and power of free; category heuristics are rules of thumb for a quick, satisfactory decision within a category, and social proof is the tendency to follow others' opinions and behaviour.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's research found that consumers who do not use AI pinball between exploration and evaluation, while AI users start a purchase journey mostly exploring and then move on to evaluating, a path that looks more like a funnel.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: The speaker called the marketing funnel a useful common language for strategy but not the reality of how consumers decide.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: The third benefit, suggestion, is that AI often proposes ideas, brands and products a consumer had not thought of, which lowers the cost of curiosity.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's research found that people who use AI run more searches than people who do not.

sources.title: Expanding AI Overviews and introducing AI Mode

author: Google blog (5 March 2025)
label: docs
text: Google's AI Mode launch post (March 2025) said that with Google's new AI features people are using Google Search more than ever, as they get help with new and more complex questions.

sources.title: Expanding AI Overviews and introducing AI Mode

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google's research found that people who use AI also visit more brand websites, because it is simply easier.
quote: the people that are using AI, they search more, and they also visit more websites of brands.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's AI features guide says that with AI Overviews people have been visiting a greater diversity of websites for help.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: AI users sometimes take even longer purchase journeys, but they perceive their journeys as shorter, a perception the data does not always support (part of this passage is uncertain in the recording).

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: For high-risk or high-involvement purchases, ease, assistance and suggestion are often not enough, and consumers add a reassurance step to reduce the risk of the decision.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: After exploring with AI, people often go back to Google Search and to the websites of the product or service providers to double-check before buying, for example trust in the company and cancellation policies.

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether content presents information in a way that makes you want to trust it, such as clear sourcing, evidence of expertise and background about the author or the site, for example through an author page or the site's About page.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: slide
text: Google's slide defined the brand heuristic as a cognitive shortcut in which consumers use a brand's name and reputation as a proxy for product quality, reliability and value.
quote: A cognitive shortcut where consumers use a brand's name and reputation as a proxy for product quality, reliability, and value

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: In the reassurance step the brand heuristic is especially important: a brand familiar to the consumer conveys a lot of information and confidence.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

author: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)
label: docs
text: Google's messy-middle report says leading brands keep a meaningful share of consumer preference even against competitors with much better offers, and calls brand one of the strongest heuristics in consumer choice.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: A new or less familiar brand should expect people to double-check it and should prepare assets that give them the extra reassurance they need at that last step.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: slide
text: A Google slide showed nine Google Trends charts of trust-checking searches in several markets and languages (source line: Google Trends, January 2016 to March 2026, web search), all rising toward the end of the range: 'is [brand] legit?' (two panels), '[brand] è affidabile?', '[brand] jest bezpieczne?', 'Is [brand] betrouwbaar?', 'Ist [brand] seriös?', '[brand] est fiable?', '¿es [brand] falso?' and 'trustpilot'.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Google Trends shows a rise since about 2020 in searches of the form 'is [brand] legit', in the UK and in most other countries Google looked at.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: The speaker read the rise in 'is [brand] legit' searches as a signal that people go back to the brand's website and to Google Search to take an extra reassurance step.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Consumers who use AI no longer feel frustrated by a lack of progress in a purchase decision; they feel they are moving through the funnel and feel like category experts.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Consumers boosted by AI in their purchase decisions were still a small group in October 2026, but the group is growing as more people start using AI (the word 'boosted' is an uncertain reading at this point of the recording).

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: slide
text: Google's marketing research talk reached the same advice as Search: optimise for people to win in generative AI search.
quote: Optimise for people to win in generative AI search

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: The reason given for optimising for people was that a human still makes the final purchase decision, so content has to be useful to that person.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: slide
text: Google's slide advised producing unique, helpful, human-centric content.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's guide for generative AI features says creating content that people find unique, compelling and useful will likely influence a website's presence in generative AI search.

sources.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: slide
text: Google's slide advised partnering with category opinion formers, such as YouTube creators, experts and institutions, who can give consumers extra reassurance.

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: Because purchase journeys can be long and competitive, brands should be present where decisions are made: on Google Search and on their own brand website.

sources.title: Marketing in the messy middle
sources.publisher: Think with Google (Google and The Behavioural Architects; Decoding Decisions, part 2)

speaker: Pablo Pérez
label: stage
text: A brand's own website matters in AI-assisted journeys because it is the one source where the brand speaks in its own voice and controls the message.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: For high-involvement products and services, make the double-check easy on your own site: company details, reviews, cancellation and return policies, guarantees and contact options should be on crawlable, indexable pages linked from product and service pages.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Track trust queries about your brand, such as '[brand] legit', '[brand] reviews' or '[brand] seriös', in Search Console and Google Trends for each market, and answer them on the site, for example with a trust or about page, instead of leaving the answer to third-party review sites.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The messy-middle findings come from Google's marketing research on consumer behaviour, not from Search documentation; they describe how people decide, not how Google ranks pages, and none of them is a ranking signal.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's finding that AI users visit more brand websites is Google's own research; check it against your own data, such as branded and direct traffic in analytics and the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, before planning on it.

author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Content that helps AI-assisted shoppers names the few features that decide a category (for a phone, battery and camera), compares options on them and shows what similar buyers chose, which matches the ease, assistance and suggestion benefits Google described.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google presented its processing times for crawling, indexing and serving as an experiment: estimates from its internal logs, meant to be informative and not something to obsess about, with feedback from the audience invited.
quote: if you have an engineering mindset, then you can put a number to it.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Each of Google's processing-time charts marks a minimum, a typical value and an end point on a scale from seconds to one year, with a dotted line for corner cases, and carries the footnote that the times are estimations based on internal analysis.
quote: Times expressed on the diagram are estimations based on internal analysis.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that discovering a new URL takes about 20 hours on average across all sites it knows of, with a minimum of seconds.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google's crawl chart says the discovery of a new URL can take weeks or never happen, because the web is huge.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google said it knows hundreds of trillions of URLs (as of October 2026).

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google does not crawl all the URLs it knows, because crawling everything would generally waste resources and a much smaller crawl space is enough.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that refreshing (recrawling) a known URL takes about 30 days on average, with a minimum of seconds and an end point of weeks to never.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google's index drops URLs that have not been recrawled for a very long time, which is the 'never' end of the refresh estimate.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: For news sites in particular, Google said the refresh of a known URL can literally take seconds (the reading 'news sites' is likely but not certain).

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member reported recrawl intervals on one very large, popular client site: the homepage about 5 times a day, first-level pages about every 1.5 days (uncertain reading), and pages clustered as soft 404s every 160 to 190 days, adding that other sites will differ.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: audience
label: stage
text: An audience member said that on the large site they observed, recrawl frequency followed the site hierarchy, demand and how well each page is internally linked.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: With a typical refresh of about 30 days and deep or soft-404-like pages recrawled only every few months, link important deep pages from strong hub pages and fix pages that look like errors; then check recrawl intervals by site depth in server logs or the Crawl Stats report.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that processing a sitemap takes about 24 hours on average, with a minimum of minutes.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: If a sitemap is useful to Google and the site is of high quality, Google tries to refetch the sitemap within 14 days at most.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google may never fetch a lower-quality site's sitemap again: once it figures out the site is of lower quality, it no longer wants to fetch the sitemap.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a robots.txt update is picked up in about 24 hours, with a minimum of seconds and an end point of 25 hours on the slide.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google said its service level objective is to refresh robots.txt every 24 hours, as RFC 9309 calls for, though delays happen now and then.

sources.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: A site owner can submit robots.txt in Search Console to force Google to refresh it sooner.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Plan robots.txt changes a day ahead, because Google may use the old file for about 24 hours; for an urgent change, request a refresh in Search Console instead of waiting.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google's crawl chart puts a crawl capacity update at seconds when backing off, typically 4 hours or 1-2 weeks, and 1-3 weeks in recovery.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: When a site starts serving 500 errors, Google lowers the crawl capacity allocated to the site within about four hours on average.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Increases in crawl capacity take longer than decreases, within one to three weeks, because Google first needs to know that the higher demand will last.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: A continuously running process recalculates each site's crawl capacity within a month, so a capacity change takes up to about a month at most.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Spoken and slide figures for capacity increases differ (one to three weeks, up to a month, versus 1-2 weeks typical and 1-3 weeks in recovery), but the lesson is the same: a burst of 5xx errors cuts crawling within hours and recovery takes weeks, so keep servers stable before launches and migrations.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a crawl demand update driven by Search takes about 20 hours on average, with a minimum of minutes and an end point of weeks to months.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: When Google notices the web getting excited about a few URLs on a site, it allocates more crawl demand to the whole site so it does not miss content useful to future searchers.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Crawl demand can also come from other Google products, such as Shopping, and the roughly 20-hour estimate covers only demand from Search.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that rendering takes seconds when done right away and hours when the page waits in the queue, with an end point of days to weeks.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google renders pages in two ways: immediately after crawling, or later through a queue-based process that runs elsewhere.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Content that JavaScript adds to a page is typically seen by Google's indexing system within a few hours, and at worst within weeks.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said Google keeps saying it renders every URL on the internet and that he would say this is not true, though it is what he was told; he went on to say that Google's logs show the rendering queue cleared within weeks.
quote: we keep saying that we render every single URL on the internet. I would say that that's not true

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: According to Google's logs, everything in the rendering queue gets rendered within weeks.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Put critical content, links and meta tags in the server HTML: content that needs JavaScript reaches indexing only after rendering, usually within hours but sometimes weeks, and even Google's own speaker doubted that every URL gets rendered.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that meta annotations, such as robots meta tags, are processed in typically 45 to 90 minutes, with a minimum of 200 seconds (about three minutes) and an end point of 1 to 4 days.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Meta annotation processing is a critical step of indexing: until a document passes it, Google cannot go on indexing the document.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that link annotations are processed in minutes to 1-3 weeks, with an end point of about one year on the slide.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that indexing a document end to end takes about 1.5 hours on average, with a minimum of seconds.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google defined indexing end to end as the time from a document entering indexing until its critical processes finish and it reaches the serving index, tokenized and ready to be served as a result.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google's indexing chart says end-to-end indexing can take months or never happen, for reasons of quality.

sources.title: Ask Google to recrawl your URLs

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said the 1.5-hour indexing average is probably lowered by selection bias, because so many news sites push out articles.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: By Google's own averages, getting found and crawled takes far longer than indexing (about 20 hours to discover a URL and 30 days to refresh one, against 1.5 hours to index), so for faster results work on discovery: internal links from often-crawled pages and accurate sitemaps.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: After Google processes a page that now returns a 404 or a noindex, it usually removes the page from its serving index within one to three weeks, sometimes much sooner.

sources.title: How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: A change of canonical URL usually takes one to three weeks to show, though it can happen in seconds because Google allocates enough resources to canonicalization.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said he had updated Google's documentation about canonicalization changes about a month before the event (around early September 2026).

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google treats a site move as a complex canonicalization process in which every signal of the old site is recalculated and moved to the new one, and every indexing process has to run.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: A site move can finish within a few weeks for a small site, takes one to three months on average, and in the worst case about a year.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said a site move can take up to about a year in the worst case, because Google's slowest signal is recalculated only about once a year (some words of this passage are uncertain readings).

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Keep migration redirects in place for at least a year and judge a site move after one to three months, not days: Google's speaker said its slowest signal needs about a year to be recalculated (a partly uncertain passage of the recording), and Google's site move guide says to keep redirects generally at least one year.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google usually picks up structured data updates within hours to one or two weeks, sometimes immediately.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google may never use structured data from a site it does not trust: once it sees markup it does not trust, it does not touch it.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google indexes images in hours to two days on average, and the fastest it can reliably index an image is under 150 seconds.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google tries to index images from news sites much faster than usual, which lowers the average image indexing time (the reading 'news sites' is likely but not certain).

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google's deep analysis of a video, needed to actually understand it, can take months to finish.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a removal requested by the site owner in Search Console takes effect in about 2 hours on average, from minutes up to 24 hours.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Search Console removals average about 2 hours because Google pushes removals out to its serving system about every 2 hours.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: To hide a URL from Google Search urgently, use the Removals tool in Search Console (about 2 hours) and also add a noindex or a 404, which takes one to three weeks to drop the page from the index.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a snippet update takes 1-2 days on average and up to several weeks to months, because the page has to be reprocessed to extract the new text.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that updating the image shown with a text result takes 1-2 weeks on average, from a minimum of days up to several weeks to months.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: The image shown with a text result changes only after the image itself is indexed or reindexed and then goes through a further processing step involving embeddings.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a title update takes as long as a snippet update: 1-2 days on average, up to several weeks to months.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: After changing a title or meta description, wait at least a few days before judging the result in Search; if nothing changes after several weeks, check that the page was recrawled, since snippets and titles are only re-extracted from a reprocessed page.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that removing a manual action after a reconsideration request takes 1-2 weeks on average, at least 2-3 days, and 4-6 weeks or much longer for dormant sites.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: For some sites a manual action is almost never removed, because the owners do not make the effort to actually clean up the site.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a core update affects a site within 2 to 4 weeks from the beginning of its rollout.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Recovery after a core update typically takes 3 to 6 months once the site has put in work to regain traffic, and up to 6 months to a year, until the next core update.

sources.title: Google Search's core updates and your website

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: slide
text: Google estimated that a spam update affects sites within 1-2 days of the rollout, 1-2 weeks for continuous processing (said on stage as 2 weeks on average) and months for batch refreshes.

sources.title: Google Search spam updates and your site

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Set expectations for recovery work: a manual action can lift within weeks of a real clean-up, but recovery from a core update typically takes 3 to 6 months and may need the next core update, so do not judge quality work within the first weeks.

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google's processes depend on each other: crawling happens first, then indexing, then serving, so a change such as a new canonical cannot be processed until the page has been recrawled.

sources.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

session: How long does it take to..?
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google said it structured the three days of the event as crawling, indexing and serving because that is literally how Search works.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Central, Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Google's robots.txt guide says its crawlers update their cached copy of a site's robots.txt every 24 hours, and that the Request a recrawl option in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it faster.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google
label: docs
text: Google's crawl rate guide says that when a significant number of URLs return 500, 503 or 429, Google reduces the site's crawl rate, which starts increasing again automatically once the errors drop; it warns against doing this for longer than 1-2 days.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's guide to fixing canonicalization issues says that even after content issues are fixed, Google might hold pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks, and that pages split out faster when they differ clearly and significantly.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The canonicalization documentation update mentioned on stage appears in Google's documentation changelog on 10 July 2026 (re-evaluation time, page last updated 21 August 2026), earlier than 'about a month' before the event; its 'up to two weeks' sits at the short end of the one to three weeks said on stage.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's site move guide says to keep redirects for as long as possible, generally at least one year, so that Google can transfer all signals to the new URLs.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's site move guide says that, as a general rule, a small to medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move and larger sites take longer, depending on the number of URLs and server speed.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Google's Removals tool help says a temporary removal request usually takes up to a day to process and lasts only about six months, so the content must also be removed permanently, for example with a 404 or 410, a noindex or a password.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Console Help
label: docs
text: Google's Manual actions report help says most reconsideration reviews take several days or weeks, and that some, such as link-related requests, may take longer.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Google Search Central
label: docs
text: Google's title link guide says Google has to recrawl and reprocess a page to notice changes to the sources of its title link, which may take a few days to a few weeks.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.

session: How long does it take to..?
author: Ibrahim Anjro
label: analysis
text: Google's ranking systems guide speaks of hundreds of billions of pages in its Search index; by the author's arithmetic, against the hundreds of trillions of URLs Google said it knows, only around one known URL in a thousand is indexed, if both figures are taken at face value.

sources.title: A guide to Google Search ranking systems

session: Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google said there is so much going on in Search that AI topics were covered across the event only where contextually important, and its closing message was to use AI but understand how it works so as to use it responsibly.

session: Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Google described AI as an umbrella of many technologies working together, one of which is machine learning: systems that learn from large amounts of data to make informed decisions.

session: Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Gary Illyes said machine learning is about 50 years old and that Google has been using it for 'probably 30 years', starting with statistical models that made the 'Did you mean' feature possible.

session: Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything.
speaker: Gary Illyes
label: stage
text: Some of Google's search ranking features are plain machine learning models, because for some tasks simple machine learning models are more useful than large language models.

sources.title: A guide to Google Search ranking systems
